de/dialogue/ef/ef87fa785bd211d7.mp3.text:
f:Die Zeitkapsel wird erst im Jahr 2050 geöffnet. Was glaubt ihr, wie die Welt dann aussieht?
m:Bis dahin werden Roboter die meisten Hausarbeiten übernommen haben – hoffentlich auch das Aufräumen.
f:Ich bin da skeptischer. Vieles, was man vor dreißig Jahren vorhergesagt hat, ist nie eingetreten.
f:Guter Punkt. Und was werden die Leute wohl denken, wenn sie eure Briefe lesen?
m:Sie werden sich bestimmt über unsere Handys amüsieren. Bis dahin wird man sie längst durch etwas anderes ersetzt haben.
f:Und vielleicht werden sie das Klimaproblem bis dahin gelöst haben. Das wäre mein größter Wunsch.
f:Apropos Briefe: Wo ist eigentlich Jonas? Er wollte doch heute seinen Brief mitbringen.
m:Er wird den Bus verpasst haben. Das passiert ihm fast jeden Montag.
f:Oder er wird den Brief zu Hause vergessen haben und holt ihn gerade.
f:Na gut, bis zur Pause wird er schon gekommen sein. Fangen wir mit euren Prognosen an.
m:Meine Prognose: In fünfundzwanzig Jahren werde ich meinen eigenen Brief nicht wiedererkennen – oder mich für ihn schämen!

de/dialogue/f1/f1e08077c3c77956.mp3.text:
m:Ich wohne erst seit drei Monaten hier. Bist du eigentlich in Mannheim aufgewachsen?
f:Ja, ich bin ein echtes Mannheimer Kind – in der Neckarstadt geboren und in der Innenstadt zur Schule gegangen.
m:Und deine Familie? Entschuldige, wenn die Frage zu persönlich ist.
f:Kein Problem. Meine Eltern sind in den Achtzigern aus einer kleinen Stadt am Schwarzen Meer gekommen.
m:Fragen dich eigentlich viele Leute danach, oder bin ich da gerade ein typischer Fall?
f:Ständig. Die typische Frage ist: "Und woher kommst du wirklich?" Dabei ist Mannheim eine völlig richtige Antwort.
m:Bei mir ist es eher umgekehrt: Ich bin hier noch nicht angekommen. Mir fehlt die kleine Dorfgemeinschaft.
f:Was genau vermisst du denn am meisten an deinem alten Leben im Schwarzwald?
m:Im Dorf kannte jeder jeden. Hier grüßt mich im Treppenhaus kaum jemand, nicht einmal die direkten Nachbarn.
f:Gib der Stadt eine faire Chance. Mit ein paar guten Freunden fühlt man sich schnell zugehörig.
m:Und was ist Heimat für dich – ein bestimmter Ort, eine Sprache oder bestimmte Menschen?
f:Ehrlich gesagt alles zusammen: das Türkisch von meiner Oma, der Mannheimer Dialekt und der Geruch von frischem Simit.

de/dialogue/fa/fa596e894287483a.mp3.text:
f:Herzlich willkommen! Frau Peters, haben es die Jugendlichen heute leichter oder schwerer als Ihre Generation?
f:In mancher Hinsicht leichter. Wir Älteren hatten weniger Möglichkeiten, aber dafür auch weniger Druck.
m:Das stimmt. Viele Gleichaltrige in meinem Freundeskreis haben Angst, keine bezahlbare Wohnung zu finden.
f:Als ich jung war, bekam fast jeder Berufsanfänger schnell eine eigene Wohnung. Das kann man sich heute kaum vorstellen.
f:Herr Sayed, was ärgert Sie am meisten an den Vorurteilen gegenüber jungen Leuten?
m:Dass man uns oft für faul hält. Die meisten Auszubildenden, die ich kenne, arbeiten im Schichtdienst.
f:Das finde ich auch ungerecht. Faule und Fleißige gab es schon immer, in jeder Generation.
f:Und gibt es etwas, das die beiden Generationen voneinander lernen könnten?
m:Auf jeden Fall. Frau Peters erzählt so viel Interessantes aus ihren dreißig Jahren auf der Werft.
f:Und ich habe von ihm etwas ganz Neues gelernt: Videotelefonie mit meiner Enkelin in Kanada!
f:Das ist doch das Schönste an solchen Begegnungen. Vielen Dank, Ihnen beiden!

en/dialogue/01/018212f4b8b99fe0.mp3.text:
m:Today's guest has spent ten years growing meat in a lab. Ingrid, how exactly is cultivated meat made?
f:A small sample of cells is taken from a living animal, and the cells are grown in large steel tanks.
m:And the animal isn't harmed? That's what many of our listeners have been asking.
f:No. The sample is taken painlessly, and no animals need to be slaughtered at all.
m:Has cultivated meat been approved for sale anywhere yet?
f:It's been approved in a few countries, and more applications are being reviewed as we speak.
m:Critics say it should be tested for years before it's sold to the public. Is that fair?
f:Safety must be taken seriously, of course. Every product is checked far more strictly than ordinary meat.
m:What about farmers? Some people worry that their jobs will be replaced by laboratories.
f:That's a real concern. Ideally, farmers would be involved in the new industry instead of being left behind.
m:And will it be labeled clearly? People want to know what they're eating.
f:Absolutely. Customers mustn't be misled. In my view, the word "cultivated" should be printed on every package.

f:And what exactly are you responsible for at the moment?
m:I deal with complaints, and recently I've been training new staff as well.
f:How many people have you trained so far?
m:About twenty, I think. I really enjoy helping new people find their feet.
f:That's impressive. So why do you want to leave the company?
m:I've been doing the same job for years. I'm ready for a new challenge.
f:I understand. And what would you say is your biggest weakness?
m:Public speaking. I've been taking an evening course to get better at it.
f:Good to hear. Last question: what's your notice period?
m:One month, so I could start at the beginning of June.

en/dialogue/16/169a826b129e8fa6.mp3.text:
f:Have you seen the new report from the education department? It says most of our students use AI tools for homework.
m:I read it last night. Around seventy percent of teenagers are believed to use chatbots at least once a week.
f:It's often said that these tools make students lazy. Do you think that's true?
m:Not necessarily. Students who use them well are thought to learn faster, because they get instant feedback.
f:But half the essays I'm marking sound identical, and one of them is known to have been copied word for word.
m:That's a real problem. The detection tools are claimed to be accurate, but they've been known to accuse innocent students.
f:So banning AI completely isn't the answer either. Students will be expected to use it at university anyway.
m:Exactly. It's generally agreed that we should teach them to use it critically instead.
f:What would that look like in practice, in your subject?
m:Students could be asked to compare a chatbot's answer with a textbook and find the mistakes.
f:I like that. Chatbots are known to make things up sometimes, so the students would learn to check their sources.
m:Let's suggest it at Monday's staff meeting. If nothing else, it'll make for a lively discussion.

en/dialogue/25/25ba1279c4bf44ba.mp3.text:
f:Welcome back to Tech Talk. With me is Callum Reid, who researches image manipulation at a university in Glasgow. Callum, a listener emailed us this week. She saw a photo of a shark swimming down a flooded highway and shared it before realizing it might be fake. How common is that?
m:Extremely common. That particular image, or versions of it, has appeared after almost every major flood for over a decade. And every time, someone claims that it was taken that very morning.
f:So how can ordinary people tell whether a photo is genuine?
m:The first thing I'd suggest is a reverse image search. You upload the picture, and the search engine shows you where else it has appeared. If it was online five years ago, it obviously wasn't taken yesterday.
f:That sounds simple. What about photos that have been edited, or created from scratch?
m:Look for details that don't make sense: shadows falling in different directions, text on signs that's blurred or meaningless, hands with too many fingers. AI-generated images used to be easy to spot because of things like that, but they're improving fast.
f:Which makes me wonder whether we'll be able to tell at all in a few years' time.
m:Honestly, I think spotting fakes by eye is bound to become harder. That's why many experts are urging news organizations and camera makers to attach verified information to genuine photos — a kind of digital signature that shows where and when a picture was taken.
f:Some listeners have told us they've simply stopped trusting anything they see online. Is that a sensible reaction?
m:I understand it, but I'd warn people against going too far. If you believe nothing, you'll ignore real warnings too, and in a genuine emergency, that can be dangerous. What we need is healthy skepticism, not cynicism.
f:So, what's your advice for our listener with the shark photo?
m:Don't feel bad — she's in very good company. Next time, pause before sharing. Ask who posted it first and whether a reliable source has reported the same thing. And if it seems too extraordinary to be true, it probably is.
f:Callum Reid, thank you for joining us.
m:My pleasure.

en/dialogue/3c/3c4adacd3b4271ad.mp3.text:
f:Can you believe it's been two years since the robots arrived? I was sure we'd all be out of work by now.
m:Honestly, if the company hadn't offered the retraining program, I would have left the same week.
f:Me too. If I hadn't learned to program the machines, I'd probably have ended up stacking shelves somewhere else.
m:Do you remember Pieter? He refused to take the course, and he was made redundant six months later.
f:It's a shame. If he'd given it a chance, he might have kept his job.
m:Maybe. But he'd been lifting boxes here for thirty years. He might not have enjoyed staring at screens all day.
f:True. Still, the work is far less physical now. My back would have given up years ago if I'd kept lifting boxes.
m:And the pay is better. I wouldn't have been promoted if I hadn't picked up those new skills.
f:What worries me is the next wave. People say software will take over planning and scheduling too.
m:Then we'll have to upskill again. Lifelong learning isn't optional anymore, is it?
f:No. If someone had told me that at school, I would have laughed at them.
m:And if someone had told me I'd end up teaching robots, I'd have laughed even harder!

en/dialogue/3d/3d9262eb15dc4a25.mp3.text:
m:Welcome, everyone. Tonight's motion is that the university should stop serving beef on campus. Hana, you're speaking first.
f:Thank you. What we're asking for is a small change with a big effect. Beef has the highest carbon footprint of any common food.
m:Lucas, you're opposing the motion. What's your main objection?
m:It isn't the goal that I disagree with — it's the method. What worries me is that bans tend to make people defensive.
f:But voluntary measures have been tried for years. What happened was that sales of plant-based meals barely changed.
m:The reason why they didn't change is that the vegetarian options were expensive and, frankly, not very tasty.
f:I'll concede that point. But the thing that surprised me most was how many students supported a ban in our survey.
m:So, Lucas, what would you do instead?
m:What I'd do is make the plant-based meals cheaper and better, and then let students choose for themselves.
f:All we're saying is that the university should lead by example. It's institutions, not individuals, that can change habits fastest.
m:And it's students who'll decide whether they eat on campus or buy a burger across the road.
m:Two very clear positions. Before we vote, let's take some questions from the audience.

en/dialogue/3e/3e04000fad9ef71a.mp3.text:
f:Hi! Can I help you?
m:Yes, please. I bought this jacket here on Saturday, but there's a problem with it.
f:Oh no. What's wrong with it?
m:The zipper is broken. Look — it doesn't close.
f:You're right. I'm sorry about that. Do you have the receipt?
m:Yes, here it is. I paid by card.
f:Thanks. Would you like a refund, or do you want to exchange it?
m:I really like the jacket, so I'd like to exchange it.
f:No problem. Let me check… I'm afraid we don't have it in black anymore. We only have green or gray.
m:Oh. Could I try the gray one?
f:Of course. Here you are. The fitting room is over there.
m:Thanks… Hmm, it's a little tight. Do you have it in a large?
f:Just a moment… Yes, here's a large in gray.
m:Perfect. This one fits me much better.
f:Great. Is there anything else I can help you with?
m:Yes, actually. These gloves were a gift, but they're too small for me. Can I return them? I don't have a receipt.
f:I'm sorry, we can't give you a refund without a receipt, but we can give you store credit.
m:That's fine. Thank you for your help!

en/dialogue/3f/3fe917a450a3cb86.mp3.text:
m:You look happy. Did something good happen at work?
f:Kind of. My colleague Ben told me he'd deleted all his social media apps.
m:Really? He's always on his phone. Why did he do that?
f:He said he was spending four hours a day scrolling, and he felt anxious.
m:Four hours! That's half a working day. So how does he feel now?
f:He told me he was sleeping much better and reading books again.
m:Good for him. But doesn't he miss all his friends' updates?
f:He said that his real friends would call him if they had news.
m:Fair point. Let me check my screen time… Oh no. Six hours yesterday!
f:Ha! I said exactly the same thing when I saw mine.
m:OK, let's try a challenge. No phones in the kitchen for a week.
f:Deal. But last month you told me you couldn't live without your phone!

en/dialogue/45/4508bc5f762843b8.mp3.text:
f:Good morning, and welcome to City Talk. My guest today is Martin Reyes, the principal of Westbrook High School, which banned phones during the school day last September. Martin, thanks for coming in.
m:Thanks for having me.
f:So, why did you decide to ban phones?
m:Well, our teachers had been complaining for years. Students were checking their phones in every class, and at lunchtime the cafeteria was completely silent. Everyone was just looking at a screen.
f:How does the ban actually work?
m:When students arrive in the morning, they put their phones in a locker, and they get them back at three o'clock. If parents need to contact their kids, they call the school office.
f:I imagine the students weren't very happy about that.
m:No, not at first! In the first week, a lot of students told me they felt anxious without their phones. One girl said she didn't know what to do with her hands.
f:And now?
m:Now it's very different. The cafeteria is noisy again, which I love. Students are playing cards, chatting, even reading. And our teachers say that students concentrate much better in class.
f:What about the parents? Were they worried?
m:Some were. A few parents asked me whether their children would be safe without a phone. We explained that the office is always open, and that seemed to help.
f:Has the ban had any effect on grades?
m:It's too early to say for sure, but our test results this spring were the best we've had in five years.
f:Would you recommend the idea to other schools?
m:Yes, but I'd say: talk to parents and students first, and explain why you're doing it. If people understand the reasons, they're much more likely to accept the rules.
f:Martin Reyes, thank you very much.
m:My pleasure.

en/dialogue/47/476b270472a05764.mp3.text:
m:So, Aditi, your review is on Thursday. Have you decided what you're going to ask for?
f:I'm thinking of asking for a ten percent raise. I've taken on two extra projects since my last review.
m:Good. Do you have evidence? Numbers are far more persuasive than telling them how hard you've worked.
f:I do. The app redesign I led increased sign-ups by thirty percent. If I hadn't pushed for user testing, we would have launched the old version.
m:Then start with that. Open with the results, not the request. What will you say if your manager tells you there's no budget?
f:Honestly, that's what I'm dreading. Last year I just said "OK" and left the room.
m:This time, have a plan B. You could accept a smaller raise now, provided that your salary is reviewed again in six months.
f:Or extra training. I'd really like to do a course in data visualization.
m:Good idea. Training usually costs the company less than a raise, so it's easier for them to say yes. But don't offer it too early — let them make the first counteroffer.
m:Exactly. Supposing they really can't offer more money, what would you accept instead?
f:A training budget, or one remote day a week. As long as I get one of those, I'd be happy.
m:That's a strong position. And one more thing: don't fill the silence. After you name your figure, stop talking.
f:That's going to be hard! I always end up apologizing for asking.
m:Everyone does at first. If I'd known that when I was your age, I'd have earned a lot more in my twenties.
f:OK, let's practice. You be my manager. "I'd like to discuss my salary, if that's all right."
m:"Of course. But I should tell you that budgets are very tight this year."
f:"I understand. However, since my last review, the redesign I led has increased sign-ups by thirty percent. On that basis, I'd like to propose a ten percent increase."
m:Perfect. Now, silence… See? It's uncomfortable, but it works.
f:It really is uncomfortable. But I think I can do it.
m:Just remember: the worst they can say is no. And even then, you'll have shown them that you know your value.

en/dialogue/49/499c14d98e972e38.mp3.text:
m:You look exhausted, Ruby. Is everything OK?
f:Not really. I'm completely stressed out — I have three deadlines this week.
m:I know the feeling. Do you take any breaks during the day?
f:Not usually. I'm the kind of person who works through lunch.
m:That's the worst thing you can do! Your brain needs a rest.
f:I know. Is there anything that helps you switch off?
m:I use an app that reminds me to stand up and breathe every hour.
f:Really? And does it actually make a difference?
m:It does. And I go to a yoga class which starts at six, after work.
f:I've never done yoga. I'm not someone who can sit still for long.
m:The teacher is a woman who used to be a lawyer, so she understands stress!
f:OK, you've convinced me. Can I come with you on Thursday?

en/dialogue/50/50a5487e4c5e1b16.mp3.text:
f:OK, everyone, shall we get started? There are three items on the agenda today, and the main one is the office move.
m:Sorry, Helen, before we start — who's taking the minutes?
f:Good question. Tomás, could you do it this time?
m:Sure, no problem.
f:Thanks. So, as you know, we've been looking for a new office for about six months. I'm happy to say we've finally found one. It's on Harbor Street, right next to the train station.
m:That's great news. Our current building is so far from public transportation.
f:Exactly. However, there's one problem. The new office is smaller, so we'll have fewer desks than people.
m:How many fewer?
f:We'll have thirty desks for forty people. As a result, we'll need to introduce flexible working. Some people will work from home two days a week.
m:I think most people will be happy with that. I've been working from home on Fridays anyway.
m:What about the moving date?
f:Unfortunately, the building won't be ready until the end of March, so we'll move on the first weekend of April.
m:And will we have to pack everything ourselves?
f:No, a moving company will do that. But you'll need to clear your desks by Thursday, March 30.
m:OK. I'll add that to the action points.
f:Great. The next item is the summer party, but I suggest we postpone that discussion until next week, as we're running out of time.
m:Fine by me.
f:So, to sum up: we move in April, we'll introduce flexible working, and everyone needs to clear their desk by March 30. Tomás, can you send the minutes to everyone by tomorrow?
m:Will do.
f:Thanks, everyone. Let's finish there.

en/dialogue/53/53cce6ca84f07a8b.mp3.text:

f:Hi. I'd like to open a bank account, please.
m:Sure. Could I see some ID, please?
f:Of course. Here's my passport.
m:Thanks. Could you fill out this form and sign here?
f:No problem. Can I get my debit card today?
m:I'm afraid not. It comes by mail in about a week.
f:Next, please! How can I help you?
f:Hi. Could you send this package to Mexico, please?
f:Sure. Can you put it on the scale for me?
f:Would you like regular or express mail?
f:Regular, please. And could I have five stamps?

en/dialogue/54/545fcf5aa272b9fd.mp3.text:
f:Welcome, everyone! Tonight's class is called "Grandma's Kitchen." Each of you has brought a recipe that someone in your family used to make. Henrik, do you want to start?
m:Sure. This is a fish soup my grandmother made every Friday when I was a kid. She grew up in a fishing village in the north of Sweden.
f:Lovely. What's in it?
m:Potatoes, leeks, cream, dill and whatever fish was fresh that day. My grandmother, who never measured anything, always said, "A little of this, a little of that."
f:Ha! That's the hardest kind of recipe. So how did you work out the amounts?
m:My aunt, whose house was next door to Grandma's, remembered most of it. We tested the soup four times last month.
f:And did it taste the same?
m:Almost. The fourth one was very close. But something was still missing.
f:That often happens. Sometimes the ingredient that's missing is a person.
m:That's true. It's not the same without her stories.
f:Do you remember any of them?
m:Lots! My favorite is about the winter when the sea froze and she walked to school across the ice.
f:OK, let's get started. Where did you buy the fish?
m:At the market on Dock Street. There's a stall that's run by a couple who catch the fish themselves. Today I got some cod and a little salmon.
f:Perfect. Everyone, the first thing we need to do is chop the leeks and potatoes. Henrik, how small?
m:About the size of a sugar cube. And don't let the soup boil after you add the cream. That's the one rule my grandmother never broke.
f:Great tip. Let's go!

en/dialogue/55/5576845da27d5623.mp3.text:
f:Hi. I think I lost my backpack this morning.
m:I'm sorry to hear that. What happened?
f:I was waiting for my flight at gate twelve.
f:While I was buying a coffee, they changed the gate.
m:Oh dear. So you ran to the new gate?
f:Yes, and I left my bag on a chair.
m:What does it look like?
f:It's small and green, with a yellow tag.
m:Just a moment… Is this your bag?
f:Yes! Oh, thank you so much!
m:A cleaner found it while she was cleaning the area.

en/dialogue/56/562ef8598b8f8ed1.mp3.text:
f:So, Lisbon in August! Have you booked the flights yet?
m:Not yet. I was wondering — what if we went by train instead?
f:By train? From London? That would take two days!
m:I know. But if we took the train, our carbon footprint would be much smaller.
f:True, but it would cost a fortune. Flights are so cheap right now.
m:If we stopped in Paris and Madrid, the journey would be part of the vacation.
f:Hmm. That actually sounds fun. But I only have ten days off.
m:If we had more time, I'd take the train both ways.
f:OK, let's compromise: train there, plane back?
m:Deal. And let's stay in a guesthouse, not one of those huge hotels.
f:Good idea. If we eat at small local places, the money will stay in the community.
m:Exactly. I'll look for train tickets tonight.

en/dialogue/57/57393a85066cbdfd.mp3.text:
f:Mom and Dad's anniversary is on Friday. What are we going to get them?
m:I'm going to order flowers. I decided last night.
f:Nice. Thirty-five years — that's amazing!
m:How about a photo album with old family pictures?
f:Great idea! I'll find the photos this weekend.
m:And I'll write the card. What should I say?
f:"Happy anniversary! Best wishes and lots of love."
m:Perfect. Oh, and don't tell Mom about the album.
f:I won't tell anyone, I promise.
m:I think they'll love it. Dad will probably cry!
f:Of course he will. He cries at everything!

en/dialogue/5d/5d5b5530177fdcb9.mp3.text:
f:Tunde, that post about the dog ban has been shared forty thousand times. Have you managed to check it yet?
m:I have. The post claims that the council will ban dogs from every park in the city from next month.
f:And what did the council actually say?
m:I called their press office this morning. The spokesperson told me they were only considering a ban in two children's playgrounds.
f:So someone took a small proposal and blew it completely out of proportion. Where did the post come from?
m:An account that was created last week. The first version said the ban had been "confirmed by a council source."
f:Did you ask the spokesperson whether a decision had been made?
m:Yes. She said no decision would be made until residents had been consulted, and she said I could quote her.
f:Good. And did you ask why they hadn't published anything about it?
m:She explained that the proposal had only been discussed at a meeting two days before.
f:Right. Let's publish the fact-check today. Make it clear that the claim is false, not just exaggerated.
m:It's already drafted. I've included a screenshot that shows when the account was created, too.

f:Did you ride it to school?

f:Were you a good student?

f:So what did you do after school?
m:We played hide-and-seek in the park for hours.
f:Did Grandma let you stay out late?
m:No way! We came home before dark every day.
m:I still miss those long summer evenings.

en/dialogue/65/65923a955b2e50b8.mp3.text:
f:Did you get the letter about the heat pump grant? The government will pay up to half the cost of installation.
m:I did. Despite the grant, though, it's still going to cost us thousands. I'm not sure we can afford it.
f:I know. Even though the running costs are supposed to be lower, the upfront cost puts a lot of people off.
m:And whereas a gas boiler takes a day to fit, a heat pump can apparently take up to a week.
f:True. Nevertheless, our boiler is fifteen years old. We'll have to replace it soon anyway.
m:Fair point. And in spite of all my complaining, I do like the idea of cutting our emissions.
f:Me too. Although the policy isn't perfect, at least it's trying to make clean heating affordable.
m:Some people say the money should go to insulation first. Our house loses heat like a sieve.
f:That's a good argument. While a heat pump changes how you heat your home, insulation means you need less heat in the first place.
m:So maybe we should do both — insulation this year, and the heat pump next year.
f:Sounds sensible. It's slower, but it spreads the cost.
m:Let's talk to the Wilsons next door. In spite of their doubts, they had one installed last winter.

en/dialogue/66/66878214552bbe2e.mp3.text:
m:Thanks for meeting me, Nimmi. I'm really behind with my essays.
f:Don't worry, it happens to everyone in first year. What's the main problem?
m:I can't concentrate in my room, so I keep putting things off.
f:You should try studying in the library. It's much easier to focus there.
m:Good idea. But I also have two essays due next Friday.
f:Then you'd better talk to your tutor today and ask for an extension.
m:Won't she think I'm lazy? I don't want to make a bad impression.
f:Not at all. It's much better to ask now than to miss the deadline.
m:OK. And what about sleep? I've been going to bed at three every night.
f:That's way too late. Why don't you leave your phone in the kitchen at night?
m:That sounds hard, but I'll try. Anything else?
f:I'd recommend making a weekly plan. And don't forget to have some fun, too!

en/dialogue/6a/6a60a42f3dfd3c09.mp3.text:
m:Grandma, do you ever wish you'd done things differently? I keep thinking I made the wrong choice leaving my job.
f:Of course. I wish I had traveled more when I was young. I always said I'd go next year, and next year never came.
m:Why didn't you go, if you wanted to travel so much?
f:Money, children, fear… If only I'd been a bit braver. But I don't regret having your mother — not for a second.
m:I regret giving up the piano. I wish I hadn't listened to my friends when they said it was boring.
f:You were twelve! Everyone makes decisions like that at twelve. You could always start again, you know.
m:Maybe. As for my job, I wish my manager would listen to ideas instead of shooting them down. That's why I left.
f:Then you did the right thing. In my experience, we regret the things we didn't do more than the things we did.
m:Is that the biggest lesson you've learned?
f:That, and to stop worrying about what other people think. I wish someone had told me that at your age.
m:Then I'll tell you something too. I wish you'd stop saying you're too old to travel.
f:Ha! Fair enough. If you book the tickets, I'll pack my bag. Where shall we go?

en/dialogue/6b/6b30deb073856cc7.mp3.text:
f:Hi! Are you in the statistics class too?
m:Yes. I'm Ji-ho, an exchange student from Seoul.
f:I'm Olivia. Have you ever studied abroad before?
m:No, I haven't. This is my first time in the US.
f:Wow. So what's your major?
m:Business. I've taken two statistics courses before.
f:Lucky you! I've never taken one. I'm a bit nervous.
m:Don't worry. The professor seems really nice.
f:Have you ever been to a class with three hundred students?
m:No, never! My classes in Seoul were small.
f:Let's sit together and take notes, then.

en/dialogue/6e/6e1465d67241a723.mp3.qaTranscript: Good morning, what would you like? Hi, I'd like a kilo of tomatoes, please. Sure, anything else? Yes, some onions and some potatoes. Here you are, the apples are very fresh today. Okay, six apples, please, and some bananas. Would you like some cheese too? Yes, please, a small piece. And bread, it's from this morning. No, thanks, I've got some bread at home. Okay, that's $15. Here you are, thank you.
en/dialogue/6e/6e1465d67241a723.mp3.text:
f:Good morning! What would you like?
m:Hi! I'd like a kilo of tomatoes, please.
f:Sure. Anything else?
m:Yes, some onions and some potatoes.
f:Here you are. The apples are very fresh today.
m:OK, six apples, please. And some bananas.
f:Would you like some cheese too?
m:Yes, please. A small piece.
f:And bread? It's from this morning.
m:No, thanks. I've got some bread at home.
f:OK. That's fifteen dollars.
m:Here you are. Thank you!

en/dialogue/71/71233f1c42952325.mp3.text:
f:Kenji, you wrote adverts for fifteen years. What's the most persuasive trick in the business?
m:Making people feel they're already behind. The best ads don't just promise to solve a problem — they persuade you that you have one.
f:Like that face cream advert that claimed to "reverse ten years of aging in a week"?
m:Exactly. Thousands of customers accused the company of exaggerating, and the regulator agreed with them.
f:How did the company respond when it was investigated?
m:At first, it denied making any false claims. It even insisted on calling the results "scientifically proven."
f:And was there any real evidence behind that?
m:The "study" involved twelve people. In the end, the company admitted that it hadn't tested the cream properly.
f:Did they at least apologize to their customers?
m:They apologized for causing confusion — which isn't quite the same as apologizing for misleading people.
f:So what would you advise our listeners to do when they see a claim like that?
m:I'd urge them to read the small print and ask who paid for the research. And never trust a one-week miracle!

en/dialogue/7b/7bec2d83ae892d51.mp3.text:
f:Thanks for coming. Honestly, I almost didn't text you back.
m:I know, and I deserve that. I'm really sorry about Friday.
f:I booked a table for eight people, and you didn't even call.
m:You're right. I let you down. My phone died at work, but that's no excuse.
f:It isn't just Friday, Kwame. You cancel all the time these days.
m:That's fair. Work has been crazy, but I should make more time for you.
f:We used to see each other every week. Do you remember?
m:Of course. We'd meet at the market every Sunday and talk for hours.
f:Exactly. I don't want us to drift apart like other friends do.
m:Me neither. Let me take you out for a birthday dinner this week.
f:OK, apology accepted. But you're paying — and please don't be late!
m:Deal. And I'll charge my phone before I leave the house!

en/dialogue/7c/7ca9fc6e037fd6ac.mp3.qaTranscript: Hi, Sienna, what are you doing? I'm sitting at home, it's snowing in Toronto. Snowing? Here in Sydney it's summer. Lucky you, what's the weather like? It's sunny and very hot. And what are you doing now? I'm walking on the beach. Oh no, I'm wearing two sweaters. Ah, is it very cold? Yes it's minus 10 degrees. We there are, I love summer in January. And I love hot chocolate in January.
en/dialogue/7c/7ca9fc6e037fd6ac.mp3.text:
m:Hi, Sienna! What are you doing?
f:I'm sitting at home. It's snowing in Toronto!
m:Snowing? Here in Sydney it's summer.
f:Lucky you! What's the weather like?
m:It's sunny and very hot.
f:And what are you doing now?
m:I'm walking on the beach!
f:Oh no! I'm wearing two sweaters.
m:Ha! Is it very cold?
f:Yes, it's minus ten degrees.
m:Brr! I love summer in January!
f:And I love hot chocolate in January!

en/dialogue/81/81962aecfc0866ca.mp3.text:
f:Another parcel? That's the third one this week, Malik. What did you buy this time?
m:A smart water bottle that reminds you to drink. If I weren't so forgetful, I wouldn't have bought it.
f:To be fair, if I hadn't started my no-buy year, I'd have a wardrobe full of clothes I never wear.
m:How long have you been doing it now? It sounds exhausting.
f:Seven months. Honestly, I'd be a lot poorer now if I hadn't stopped shopping online every evening.
m:I admire that, but I'd find it really hard. All those ads make me feel I'm missing out.
f:That's exactly what they're designed to do. They're very good at turning wants into needs.
m:Fair enough. If I weren't such an easy target, I wouldn't have signed up for four streaming services either.
f:Four! If you'd canceled two of them last year, you'd have enough money for a weekend away now.
m:All right, you've convinced me. I'll cancel two tonight, and maybe I'll sell the bottle online.
f:Why not just use it? Buying something and getting rid of it straight away is wasteful too.
m:Good point. I'll keep it — and next time, I'll read the reviews before I click "buy."

en/dialogue/85/85443944c7ecedfa.mp3.text:
m:Good morning, Ms. Reyes. What seems to be the problem?
f:I have a bad cough, and I can't sleep at night.
m:I see. When did the cough start?
f:About a week ago. I also have a slight fever.
m:Let me examine you. Breathe in… and out.
m:It's a chest infection. You should take these antibiotics.
f:Should I stay at home from work?
m:Yes, you should rest for two or three days.
m:Here's your medicine. Take one pill twice a day.
f:Should I take it with food?
m:Yes, and you shouldn't drink alcohol with it.
f:Thank you. I hope I get better soon.

en/dialogue/86/86485ecf7aa18e26.mp3.text:
f:Hi, Felix! How was your weekend?
m:It was great, thanks. I visited my aunt in Duluth.
f:Oh, nice! Was the weather OK up there?
m:No, it was really cold, so we stayed in.
m:We cooked a big dinner and played board games all evening.
f:That sounds fun. My weekend wasn't very exciting.
m:Why not? What did you do?
f:I cleaned up my apartment and washed about a hundred dishes.
f:Then I watched two movies on the sofa.
m:Honestly, that sounds like a perfect weekend to me!
f:Well, it was relaxing. And on Sunday I walked by the lake.

en/dialogue/86/865b9af5f002a271.mp3.text:
m:So this is the famous one? Honestly, Aisha, it looks like a few blue squares painted by a child.
f:Look closer. Painted with dozens of thin layers, the blue changes depending on where you stand.
m:Hmm. You're right — it's almost purple from here. Who's the artist?
f:A woman called Ines Varga. Born in Budapest, she moved to Glasgow in her twenties and has lived here ever since.
m:And what's it supposed to mean? There's no title, just a number.
f:She refuses to explain her work. Having trained as an architect, she's more interested in space and light than in stories.
m:That explains the empty walls around it, I suppose. Wait — who's that man sitting on the floor in front of it?
f:He's probably doing exactly what she wants. Sitting close to it, you feel completely surrounded by the color.
m:Let me try… All right, I admit it. Seen from down here, it's actually quite moving.
f:See? Not knowing what it means is part of the experience. You bring your own meaning to it.
m:Maybe. But having paid twenty pounds for a ticket, I'd still like a little explanation!
f:Then let's go to the talk at three. Organized by the gallery, it's free for visitors.

en/dialogue/88/88e46596ade6a302.mp3.text:
m:Welcome, Noor! I'm Gareth. I'm in charge of the nurses.
f:Nice to meet you. How long have you worked here?
m:For twelve years. I started straight after college.
m:Have you worked as a receptionist before?
f:Yes, at a dental office, but only part-time.
m:Great. Your shift starts at eight, and your lunch break is at one.
f:How many customers do we see every day?
m:About forty. Some pet owners are nervous, so be kind.
f:Of course. Who's in the big office?
m:That's Dr. Morgan. She's been the boss here since 2010.
f:And the dog in the corner?
m:That's Biscuit. He's lived here since he was a puppy!

en/dialogue/8b/8b95b8512c890ec3.mp3.text:
f:You've been quiet all evening, Jonas. Is everything OK?
m:I've been offered a place on a carpentry course. It starts in September, and I have to decide by Friday.
f:Carpentry? But you've been an accountant for twelve years.
m:Exactly. And if I don't do it now, I'll still be sitting at the same desk in twenty years' time, wishing I'd tried.
f:So what's stopping you?
m:Money, mostly. The course lasts eighteen months. By the time I've finished, I'll have spent most of my savings.
f:How much would you be earning as a carpenter, compared with now?
m:Less at first, definitely. Apprentices don't earn much. But experienced carpenters who run their own business can do quite well, especially in the city.
f:Have you worked out whether you could earn a living afterward?
m:I've spoken to a few carpenters. Demand is set to grow, apparently, because so many older craftspeople are about to retire.
f:That's encouraging. And what does Sara think?
m:She's supportive, but she's worried. We're due to move into a bigger flat next year, and that's bound to cost more.
f:I understand. Can I tell you something? When I was offered a job in Lagos, I turned it down because it felt too risky. I've always regretted not going.
m:I didn't know that.
f:I don't dwell on it, but sometimes I think, if only I'd taken the plunge. Anyway, I'm not saying you should quit tomorrow. Could you do the course part-time?
m:There's an evening version, but it takes three years.
f:Three years sounds like a long time, but you'd keep your salary. And by the time you finish, you'll have built up a few clients, too.
m:That's true. I'd be exhausted, though. I'd be working all day and sawing wood all night.
f:Maybe. But you'd be exhausted doing something you actually care about.
f:And think about it this way: in five years' time, which would you regret more — trying and failing, or never trying at all?
m:Never trying. Definitely.
f:Well, there's your answer.
m:You might be right. I'll talk to Sara tonight, and I'll call the college first thing tomorrow.

en/dialogue/8b/8baca20c0f48c779.mp3.text:
f:Finn, I want to take an evening class this fall. Can you help me choose?
m:Sure. What are the options?
f:There's photography, pottery and Spanish. They're all on Tuesday or Wednesday evenings.
m:Which one is the cheapest?
f:Spanish. It's two hundred dollars for ten weeks.
f:Photography is the most expensive — four hundred and fifty. And you need a good camera.
m:Hmm. And pottery?
f:It's three hundred, and it's the closest to my apartment. I can walk there in five minutes.
m:What do the reviews say?
f:Pottery has the best reviews. People say the teacher is really funny.
m:What about Spanish?
f:The reviews are OK. But if I learn Spanish, I'll be able to talk to my neighbors.
m:That's true. When do the classes start?
f:Pottery starts on September tenth. Spanish starts a week later.
m:Well, I'm meeting my cousin on Wednesdays this fall, but I'm free on Tuesdays. If you choose a Tuesday class, I'll come with you!
f:Really? Pottery is on Tuesdays! OK, that's the best option, then.
m:Great. Let's sign up tonight.

en/dialogue/8b/8bbfa689b3fb763c.mp3.text:
f:Hello, I've received a letter saying I've been selected for jury service next month. I'm not sure what it involves.
m:It's an important civic duty. You're required to attend court for up to two weeks, starting on the date in your letter.
f:Two weeks? I work full time. Is my employer obliged to give me the time off?
m:Yes. Employers are required by law to let you attend, although they aren't obliged to pay you while you're away.
f:So I could lose two weeks' wages? That seems a bit unfair.
m:You're entitled to claim expenses for loss of earnings, as well as for travel and food, up to a daily limit.
f:That's a relief. And what if the dates are impossible? I'm supposed to be at a conference in the second week.
m:You have the right to ask for your service to be moved to a later date, but you can usually only do that once.
f:Understood. Is there anything I'm not allowed to do while I'm on a jury?
m:Jurors are prohibited from discussing the case with anyone outside the jury, and that includes posting about it online.
f:What about looking things up? I'm the kind of person who checks everything on the internet.
m:That's strictly forbidden. You must reach a decision based only on the evidence presented in court.

en/dialogue/8b/8bc75dad779f2b08.mp3.text:
f:Hi there. How can I help you?
m:Hi. I bought this kettle last week, but it doesn't work.
f:Oh, I'm sorry. Do you have the receipt?
m:Yes, here it is. Can I return it?
f:Of course. Would you like a refund or a new one?
m:A refund, please. And these jeans are for my son.
m:They don't fit him. They're too tight.
f:No problem. Do you want to exchange them?
m:Yes, please. Do you have them in a bigger size?
f:Let me check… Yes, here you are. Is your son here?
m:No, he's at school. But I can send him a photo!

en/dialogue/8c/8c05e974d1407310.mp3.qaTranscript: Hi, can I help you? Yes, please. I'm looking for some running shoes. Okay, what size are you? Ten, I think. How about these blue shoes? They're very popular. And, have you got them in black? Yes, we have. Here you are. Size ten. Thanks. Can I try them on? Of course. Sit here. Oh, they're too small. Have you got an eleven? Let me look yes, he is an 11. Perfect, these fit, how much are they? They're on sale, only 6 to 5 dollars. Great, can I pay by car? Sure.
en/dialogue/8c/8c05e974d1407310.mp3.text:
f:Hi! Can I help you?
m:Yes, please. I'm looking for some running shoes.
f:OK. What size are you?
m:Ten, I think.
f:How about these blue shoes? They're very popular.
m:Hmm. Have you got them in black?
f:Yes, we have. Here you are. Size ten.
m:Thanks. Can I try them on?
f:Of course. Sit here.
m:Oh, they're too small. Have you got an eleven?
f:Let me look… Yes! Here's an eleven.
m:Perfect. These fit. How much are they?
f:They're on sale. Only sixty-five dollars.
m:Great! Can I pay by card?
f:Sure.

en/dialogue/8c/8ca824c0098cb296.mp3.text:
f:So, Owen, tell me about your daily habits.
m:Well, I usually skip breakfast because I'm always late.
f:Hmm. And do you work out at all?
m:Not really. I sit at a desk all day.
f:You don't have to join a gym. Just walk more.
m:That's easy. Do I have to stop drinking coffee?
f:No, you don't, but two cups a day is enough.
m:And sleep? I only get about five hours.
f:That's not enough. You have to sleep more, Owen.
m:But my kids wake me up at six every day!
f:Then try to go to bed at ten.

en/dialogue/8d/8d2e9943ab9991cd.mp3.qaTranscript: Hi, I'm Danny Eller, I'm new here. Hi, Danny Eller, I'm June, welcome to the neighborhood. Thanks, is there a supermarket near here? Yes, there is, it's on Oak Street. Great, and are there any good cafes? Yes, there are two cafes in the square. Is there a gym? No, there isn't, but there's a nice part. Perfect, I love parks. And there's a bus stop next to the bank. Thank you June, that's very helpful.
en/dialogue/8d/8d2e9943ab9991cd.mp3.text:
f:Hi! I'm Daniela. I'm new here.
m:Hi, Daniela. I'm Joon. Welcome to the neighborhood!
f:Thanks! Is there a supermarket near here?
m:Yes, there is. It's on Oak Street.
f:Great. And are there any good cafés?
m:Yes, there are two cafés in the square.
f:Is there a gym?
m:No, there isn't. But there's a nice park.
f:Perfect. I love parks!
m:And there's a bus stop next to the bank.
f:Thank you, Joon. That's very helpful!

en/dialogue/8d/8de14d63f825b612.mp3.qaTranscript: Hemmed, what do you do in your free time? I love cooking, Indian food, Italian food. Really? I hate cooking. So what do you like doing? I like dancing and listening to music. What's your favorite music? Selzer, I go dancing every Friday. Cool, I don't like dancing very much. Do you like sports? Yes, I play soccer on Sundays. I like watching soccer, on TV. Oh, that's a hobby too.
en/dialogue/8d/8de14d63f825b612.mp3.text:
f:Hamid, what do you do in your free time?
m:I love cooking. Indian food, Italian food…
f:Really? I hate cooking!
m:So what do you like doing?
f:I like dancing and listening to music.
m:What's your favorite music?
f:Salsa! I go dancing every Friday.
m:Cool! I don't like dancing very much.
f:Do you like sports?
m:Yes, I play soccer on Sundays.
f:I like watching soccer — on TV!
m:Ha! That's a hobby too!

en/dialogue/8e/8e631c407bd7d143.mp3.qaTranscript: Excuse me, how can I get downtown? You can take the train or a taxi. Is the train expensive? No, it's cheap. It's five dollars. Can I buy a ticket here? Yes, you can. Use this machine. Can I pay by card? Yes, a one -way or a round -trip ticket. One -way please, which platform? Platform two. The next train is at 10 .15. And where do I get off? Get off at Clark Street, that's downtown.
en/dialogue/8e/8e631c407bd7d143.mp3.text:
f:Excuse me. How can I get downtown?
m:You can take the train or a taxi.
f:Is the train expensive?
m:No, it's cheap. It's five dollars.
f:Can I buy a ticket here?
m:Yes, you can. Use this machine.
f:Can I pay by card?
m:Yes. A one-way or a round-trip ticket?
f:One-way, please. Which platform?
m:Platform two. The next train is at ten fifteen.
f:And where do I get off?
m:Get off at Clark Street. That's downtown.

en/dialogue/8f/8f2ee32ec85ec4ff.mp3.text:
m:IT support, Connor speaking. How can I help?
f:Hi, it's Mei Lin from accounts. My laptop won't connect to the Wi-Fi.
m:OK. Can you tell me when the problem started?
f:This morning. It was working perfectly on Friday afternoon.
m:Right. Have you tried turning it off and on again?
f:Yes, twice. My phone connects fine, but the laptop says "No networks found."
m:Maybe the Wi-Fi is switched off. Is there a key with an antenna symbol?
f:Let me look… Yes, there's one above the number keys.
m:Great. Could you press it and tell me what happens?
f:Wow, it's connected! I probably pressed it by accident on Friday.
m:That happens a lot. Call me again if it stops working.

en/dialogue/90/9055086b98acd8f3.mp3.text:
m:Your English sounds so natural, Sakura. How long have you been learning it?
f:About six years. But I only started speaking it a lot when I moved here.
m:So what's your secret? I've been studying Japanese for ages.
f:I avoid watching shows in Japanese. I watch everything in English, with English subtitles.
m:I tried doing that with Japanese dramas, but I kept stopping every two minutes.
f:That's normal at first. Have you thought about joining a conversation group?
m:I'd like to, but I'm terrible at remembering new words.
f:Writing words on sticky notes helps me. I put them all over my apartment!
m:I'll try that. Did you enjoy studying grammar at school?
f:Not really. We had to memorize rules, and nobody encouraged us to speak.
m:Same here. I gave up learning French because the lessons were so boring.
f:Well, don't give up on Japanese! I promise to practice with you every week.

en/dialogue/93/931d66e91c42b63b.mp3.text:
f:So, what are you going to do after graduation?
m:I'm not sure. If I get a good job, I'll stay here.
f:And if you don't?
m:Then I'll probably go back home to Manchester.
f:I want to take a year off and travel.
m:Really? How will you afford it?
f:I'm saving up now. If I save enough, I'll go to South America.
m:That sounds amazing. What's your big dream?
f:Someday I hope to start my own business — a café.
m:If you open a café, I'll be your first customer!
f:Deal! And if it's successful, I'll give you free coffee.

en/dialogue/93/9364895bddc5eeb4.mp3.text:
m:You'll never guess what happened to me on Saturday.
f:Go on, tell me. Was it at the wedding you were going to?
m:Yes! I was driving to the hotel, and it was raining really hard.
m:I saw balloons and people in suits outside, so I parked and ran in.
f:And? What was the problem?
m:Well, a band was playing and people were dancing, but I didn't recognize anyone.
f:Oh no. Don't tell me it was somebody else's wedding!
m:Exactly! Just as I was reaching for a piece of cake, the bride walked over.
f:No way! What did you say to her?
m:I said congratulations, and she asked me how I knew her husband!
f:That's so embarrassing! So where was your friend's wedding?
m:It turned out it was at the hotel next door. I arrived just in time.

en/dialogue/94/94de8646559e5dbd.mp3.text:
m:Have you started "The Harbor" yet? Everyone at work is talking about it.
f:I finished it last night! I watched the last four episodes in one go.
m:No spoilers, please! I'm only on episode two. What did you think?
f:It starts slowly, but by episode three I was completely hooked.
m:The main character, who runs the café, is a bit annoying, isn't she?
f:At first, yes. But her story, which is told in flashbacks, explains a lot.
m:And the setting is amazing. Where was it filmed?
f:In Nova Scotia, where the director grew up. The coastline looks incredible.
m:What about the acting? The reviews I read were mixed.
f:The acting is brilliant, especially her brother, who hardly says a word.
m:OK. And the ending? Just tell me — is it happy or sad?
f:I'm not telling you! But you'll definitely want to watch season two.

en/dialogue/9b/9b0b979501963487.mp3.text:
m:Thanks for the proposal, Yasmin. We love your ideas, but to be honest, the fee is a bit beyond our budget.
f:I understand. Could you tell me roughly what figure you had in mind?
m:We were hoping to stay under four thousand pounds, including all six packaging designs.
f:That would be difficult for six designs. Supposing we reduced the number to four?
m:I'm afraid we really need all six. Would you be willing to lower your fee if we gave you more time?
f:I could come down to four and a half thousand, provided that I have eight weeks instead of five.
m:Eight weeks is fine, as long as the first two designs are ready for the trade fair in March.
f:That shouldn't be a problem. I'd also need a deposit of half the fee before I start.
m:We'd agree to that on condition that the price includes two rounds of revisions.
f:Two rounds are fine — unless you ask for major changes, which I'd charge separately.
m:That seems fair. Could we meet halfway on the fee and say four thousand two hundred and fifty?
f:You drive a hard bargain, Daniel! All right, it's a deal. Send me the contract and I'll sign it.

en/dialogue/9e/9ecfbd0c07360c5a.mp3.qaTranscript: Lynn, you get up very early. Yes, at half past five. Half past five. Why? I'm a baker. I start work at seven. Wow, I get up at nine. Luffy's you, and your class. It starts at ten. I have breakfast at a cafe. I have breakfast at the bakery. And you finish work at three? Yes, then I go to the gym. I go to bed at one in the morning. Ha, I go to bed at nine.
en/dialogue/9e/9ecfbd0c07360c5a.mp3.text:
m:Lin, you get up very early!
f:Yes, at half past five.
m:Half past five? Why?
f:I'm a baker. I start work at seven.
m:Wow. I get up at nine!
f:Lucky you! And your class?
m:It starts at ten. I have breakfast at a café.
f:I have breakfast at the bakery.
m:And you finish work at three?
f:Yes. Then I go to the gym.
m:I go to bed at one in the morning!
f:Ha! I go to bed at nine.

en/dialogue/a0/a01b1fee4bb1632e.mp3.text:
m:So, Clara, where did you grow up?
f:I was born in Santiago, in Chile.
f:I grew up there, and I left home at nineteen.
m:Why did you come to New Zealand?
f:I got a job at a hospital here in 2018.
m:Wow. Was it hard at first?
f:Yes, it was hard at first. But then I met Tomasz.
m:Is he your husband?
f:Yes! We got married three years ago.
m:That's a great story. I'm from Auckland — I never left!
f:Really? Not even for college?
m:No, I went to college ten minutes from my parents' house!

en/dialogue/a1/a19e264d95f17e6c.mp3.text:
f:Thank you all for coming. As you know, the council has proposed a reduction in the library's opening hours from next April.
m:The notice mentions "a reorganization of services." What would that mean in practice for families like mine?
f:In practice, the library would close on Mondays, and there would be a reduction in staff on weekday evenings.
f:But demand has increased since the closure of the community center. Has the council taken that into account?
f:That's a fair point. The increase in demand is one of the main reasons for this consultation.
m:My kids go to the homework club every evening. Its cancellation would be a disaster for working parents.
f:I understand. One option under consideration is the introduction of self-service hours, when no staff would be present.
f:How would that work? Many older people rely on the staff for help with forms and computers.
f:Assistance would still be available during staffed hours, and volunteers could provide additional support.
m:Then I'd like to make a proposal: keep the evenings open and close on Saturday mornings instead.
f:I'd support that. Saturday mornings are much quieter than weekday evenings, in my experience.
f:Thank you both. All proposals will be considered, and a summary of responses will be published before a final decision is made in January.

en/dialogue/a1/a1e9c24fda972d0f.mp3.text:
m:Welcome back! How was Scotland?
f:Unforgettable! Look, this is the Isle of Skye.
m:Wow, what a view! Was it cold?
f:A little, but the sun was shining that day.
m:Who's this man? Was he your tour guide?
f:Yes, that's Callum. He was telling us about the old castles.
f:And here we were hiking up a big hill.
m:Were those people swimming in the sea? In Scotland?
f:Yes! They were laughing, but the water was freezing.
m:Did you buy any souvenirs?
f:Just this scarf. And I took about five hundred photos!

en/dialogue/a1/a1fe6314f335650c.mp3.text:
f:So, how far is Quebec City from Toronto?
m:About eight hundred kilometers. That's a long drive.
f:How long does it take by train?
m:It takes about nine hours. You change in Montreal.
f:Hmm. Is there a direct flight?
m:Yes, it takes less than two hours.
f:And how much does a round-trip ticket cost?
m:Around three hundred dollars. The train is half that price.
f:We're on a budget, so let's take the train.
m:OK. What time does the morning train leave?
f:At about seven. Let's book our tickets now!

en/dialogue/a4/a4e3ce6ca381e049.mp3.text:
f:Hi, Rory! Are you free this weekend?
m:Hmm, I'm working on Saturday morning. What's up?
f:My cousin's band is playing at a café on Saturday night.
m:Oh, nice! What time are they starting?
f:At eight. Do you want to come?
m:Sure! I'm having dinner with my parents at six, but that's OK.
f:Great. Let's meet at the café at a quarter to eight.
m:Does seven thirty work for you? I want a good seat!
f:Perfect. And on Sunday I'm going hiking with Ana. Want to join?
m:I'd love to, but I'm helping my brother move.
f:No problem. See you on Saturday, then!

en/dialogue/a6/a6540b4c870c7351.mp3.text:
f:Are you going to come to the Diwali lights on Sunday?
m:Yes! What's going to happen?
f:They light thousands of lights on Belgrave Road.
f:There'll be music, dancing and food from lots of stalls.
m:It sounds amazing. Will it be very crowded?
f:Oh yes. Lots of people come every year.
m:Will it be cold at night?
f:Probably. Bring a warm jacket — you'll need it.
m:Are you going to celebrate with your family too?
f:Yes, we're going to light candles and have a big feast.
m:I'm sure it'll be an unforgettable night.

en/dialogue/a8/a85f4ddf60cd976f.mp3.text:
f:OK, we have three options for the team dinner.
m:Which one is the cheapest?
f:Luigi's. It's the cheapest, but it's also the smallest.
m:Hmm. We're twenty people. What about the Thai place?
f:It has the best reviews. The food is amazing.
m:But it's the farthest from the office, right?
f:Yes, it's about forty minutes by bus.
m:And the third one, the Harbor Grill?
f:It's the most expensive, but it's the most convenient.
m:Is it worth the money?
f:I think so. It has the biggest room and the best view.
m:OK, let's book the Harbor Grill. It's the best option.

en/dialogue/b3/b3bedff82ca060fd.mp3.text:
m:Wow, there are too many boxes in here!
f:I know. And we don't have enough shelves for my books.
m:How many books do you have?
f:About three hundred. I can't give them away!
m:OK. We have a little money left. Let's buy two more shelves.
f:Good idea. Now, chores. Who's going to do the dishes?
m:I don't have much time on weekdays. I work late.
f:Then you vacuum on Saturdays, and I do the dishes.
m:Deal. What about the trash?
f:You take it out on Mondays, and I take it out on Thursdays.
m:Perfect. Just one problem — your couch is too big for the door!

en/dialogue/b7/b7eabec4d7291715.mp3.text:
f:Grandpa, look what I found in this box — a letter dated nineteen sixty-four, addressed to you.
m:Let me see. Oh, that must have been from my brother Dylan. He'd just moved to Australia.
f:He says he "can't afford to call." Phone calls must have been incredibly expensive back then.
m:They were. We couldn't have spoken every week, the way you do with your friends.
f:People say my generation is glued to our phones, but I think you'd have loved video calls.
m:Maybe. Still, we might have valued letters more because they took weeks to arrive.
f:He mentions a job at the docks. He can't have been older than eighteen when he left.
m:Seventeen, actually. Our parents must have been worried sick, but they never showed it.
f:It's funny — people complain that young people are lazy, but he was working full time at seventeen.
m:Every generation says that about the next one. My father said exactly the same thing about me!
f:So the stereotypes haven't changed in sixty years. That's oddly reassuring.
m:It is. Now, help me find Dylan's number. I think it's time I gave him a video call.

en/dialogue/be/be2268cb44e19f6c.mp3.text:
f:Hi, Oscar! It's Jade. Do you have a minute?
m:Sure. What's up?
f:My mom turns sixty next month, and we're going to have a party for her.
f:It's going to be at my parents' house on Saturday the fourteenth. Would you like to come?
m:I'd love to! What time does it start?
f:At seven. We're going to have dinner in the garden, and then there'll be music and dancing.
m:That sounds great. Can I bring anything?
f:Oh, you don't have to bring anything.
m:Come on, I want to help. I'll make my chocolate cake.
f:Really? Mom loves your chocolate cake! Thank you.
m:What should I get her as a present?
f:Don't worry about a present. A card is perfect. She just wants all her friends to be there.
m:OK. Is it a surprise party?
f:No, she knows about it. She's already thinking about what to wear!
m:Ha! And will your brother come from London?
f:Yes, he's going to fly in on Friday. I think Mom will cry when she sees him.
m:I'm sure she will. OK, Saturday the fourteenth at seven. I'll be there.
f:Great. See you then!

en/dialogue/c1/c14058c82eae15ca.mp3.text:
f:Hi there. How can I help you today?
m:Hi. I have a terrible cold. My nose is running, and I have a sore throat.
f:Oh, I'm sorry. Do you have a fever too?
m:I don't think so. But I have a headache, and I'm really tired.
f:When did it start?
m:Two days ago. I have to work tomorrow, so I need something strong.
f:Well, no medicine can stop a cold. But these tablets will help with the headache and the sore throat.
m:How often should I take them?
f:Take one tablet every four hours. But don't take more than six in one day.
m:OK. Should I take them with food?
f:Yes, it's better with food. And you should drink lots of water and rest.
m:Can I take them with my allergy medicine?
f:What do you take?
m:Just one small pill every morning.
f:Can I see the box? … Yes, that's fine. You can take them together.
m:Great. And what about honey for my throat?
f:Hot water with honey and lemon is great. If you don't feel better in a week, you should see your doctor.
m:Thanks a lot. How much is that?
f:That's eight dollars and fifty cents, please.

en/dialogue/c7/c7afb10a8e06237d.mp3.text:
f:The time capsule goes into the ground tomorrow. Have you finished your letter to your future self?
m:Almost. It's strange to think that when we open it, we'll have been out of school for twenty years.
f:I've written that by then I'll have finished medical school, and I'll be working as a doctor somewhere rural.
m:That sounds like you. I honestly have no idea what I'll be doing. Maybe something that doesn't exist yet.
f:Like what? Designing holiday homes on the moon?
m:Why not? By then, people will probably be taking short trips into space, the way they take cruises now.
f:That sounds a bit far-fetched. I think most of us will still be worrying about rent and traffic, just like today.
m:Fair point. But surely cars will have become fully electric by then, and most of them will be driving themselves.
f:Probably. And I bet half the jobs our parents do will have disappeared.
m:Which is why I'm not making any firm predictions. What else did you put in the box?
f:A photo of our class, today's newspaper and my old phone. By then, it'll look like an antique.
m:And in twenty years' time, we'll be standing here laughing at how wrong we were about everything.

en/dialogue/c8/c8ff664978c0a357.mp3.qaTranscript: So Omar, what do you do? I'm a nurse. I work at City Hospital. Really? My brother's a nurse too. And you? What's your job? I'm an engineer. I work in a big office. Are your colleagues nice? Yes they are. They're very friendly. Are your parents engineers too? No. My mom's a teacher and my dad's retired. My parents are cooks. They've got a small restaurant. A restaurant? Great. What's the name?
en/dialogue/c8/c8ff664978c0a357.mp3.text:
f:So, Omar, what do you do?
m:I'm a nurse. I work at City Hospital.
f:Really? My brother's a nurse too!
m:And you? What's your job?
f:I'm an engineer. I work in a big office.
m:Are your colleagues nice?
f:Yes, they are. They're very friendly.
m:Are your parents engineers too?
f:No! My mom's a teacher and my dad's retired.
m:My parents are cooks. They've got a small restaurant.
f:A restaurant? Great! What's the name?

en/dialogue/cf/cf1779aeb5915034.mp3.text:
f:Customer relations, Nadia speaking. How can I help you today?
m:Good morning. I'd like to make a complaint about the eight-fifteen service from York on Tuesday.
f:I'm sorry to hear that. Could you tell me what happened?
m:The train was supposed to leave at eight-fifteen, but it was canceled at the last minute without any announcement.
f:I do apologize. Passengers should have been informed on the platform screens as soon as the decision was made.
m:Exactly. We waited forty minutes, and then we were told that a replacement bus was meant to be on its way.
f:That must have been very frustrating. Did the bus arrive in the end?
m:Eventually, but it was far too small for the number of passengers. Someone ought to have checked that.
f:You're quite right. That shouldn't have happened, and I'll pass your comments on to our operations team.
m:Thank you. I missed a hospital appointment as a result, and I'd been waiting three months for it.
f:I'm very sorry. You're entitled to a full refund, and I can also offer you a voucher as a gesture of goodwill.
m:I appreciate that. I'd also like a written response explaining what will be done to prevent this from happening again.

en/dialogue/cf/cf3d040b32661f9f.mp3.text:
f:Grandpa, have you seen "The Lighthouse Keeper"? I think you'd love it.
m:I don't think so. What's it about?
f:It's based on a true story. It happened in Scotland in the 1950s.
f:A young woman was looking after a lighthouse on a tiny island.
m:On her own? That sounds lonely.
f:Very. Her father had looked after it for years, but he had just died.
f:One night, while a terrible storm was blowing, she saw a light out at sea.
f:It turned out that a fishing boat had hit the rocks and its engine had stopped.
m:So what did she do? Did she call for help?
f:She couldn't, because the radio wasn't working. So she rowed out to them herself.
m:In a storm? That's incredibly brave. Did they all survive?
f:I won't spoil the ending. But it's definitely worth watching — I cried twice!

en/dialogue/cf/cfecc8d43095ce8f.mp3.qaTranscript: Good afternoon, babe, you little tell. How can I help you? Hello. I'd like to book a room, please. Of course. When are you going to arrive? On Friday, for two nights. A single or a double room. A double, please. How much is it? It's nine to five dollars a night. Is breakfast included? Yes, it is. Breakfast is from seven to ten. Great. Can I check in early? Yes, after 12, what's your name please? Caram had a HWDAD.
en/dialogue/cf/cfecc8d43095ce8f.mp3.text:
f:Good afternoon, Bay View Hotel. How can I help you?
m:Hello. I'd like to book a room, please.
f:Of course. When are you going to arrive?
m:On Friday. For two nights.
f:A single or a double room?
m:A double, please. How much is it?
f:It's ninety-five dollars a night.
m:Is breakfast included?
f:Yes, it is. Breakfast is from seven to ten.
m:Great. Can I check in early?
f:Yes, after twelve. What's your name, please?
m:Karim Haddad. H-A-double D-A-D.

en/dialogue/d0/d0d53e79e1e4e1bf.mp3.qaTranscript: Hello everyone, I'm Grace. Your teacher. Hi, Grace, my name's Lucia. And I'm Kenji, nice to meet you. Nice to meet you too. Are you Chinese? No, I'm not. I'm Japanese, and you? I'm Spanish. I'm from the Lancia. And where do you live now, Lucia? I live here in Toronto. Me too, but my English isn't very good. That's okay. We're here to learn.
en/dialogue/d0/d0d53e79e1e4e1bf.mp3.text:
f:Hello, everyone. I'm Grace, your teacher.
f:Hi, Grace! My name's Lucía.
m:And I'm Kenji. Nice to meet you.
f:Nice to meet you too. Are you Chinese?
m:No, I'm not. I'm Japanese. And you?
f:I'm Spanish. I'm from Valencia.
f:And where do you live now, Lucía?
f:I live here in Toronto.
m:Me too! But my English isn't very good.
f:That's OK. We're here to learn!

en/dialogue/d3/d3733e0ef4efbc23.mp3.text:
f:Luca! I didn't know you came here. Is this the gym you joined?
m:Yes, I've been coming for three months. It's the best decision I've made all year.
f:What made you start climbing? You used to hate sports.
m:My doctor told me I needed an activity I would actually enjoy.
f:And this is it? Isn't it really hard on your arms?
m:At first, yes. But the coach I train with is really patient.
f:Is that the guy you were talking to at the front desk?
m:That's him. He's the one who taught me how to fall safely.
f:I really need to get in shape. The gym I pay for is just too boring.
m:Come along on Thursday! There's a beginners' class that starts at seven.
f:Do I need special shoes, or can I wear the ones I run in?
m:They'll lend you shoes for your first session. Just bring water and a towel.

en/dialogue/d7/d7896a59d0ab490c.mp3.text:
f:Bongani! Everyone at the office misses you. How's the teacher training going?
m:It's hard work, but I love it. I've been teaching a class of eight-year-olds since January.
f:Wow. But you were doing so well in accounting. Why did you leave?
m:I was earning good money. However, I felt bored and tired every single day.
f:I complain about work all the time, but starting again sounds terrifying.
m:It was scary. I took a big pay cut, so money is tight at the moment.
f:And what did your family think about it?
m:My parents were worried. Even though they had doubts, they supported me.
f:That's great. Is there anything you miss about the old job?
m:Honestly? The salary — and the people. The coffee was much better, too!
f:Ha! So, do you have any regrets about changing careers?
m:None. I earn less now. However, I've never felt so useful in my life.

en/dialogue/d8/d809b2dcb0b639b4.mp3.text:
f:Thanks for coming, Rafael. Have you ever worked with tourists?
m:Yes, I have. I worked at a hotel in Lisbon.
f:How long did you work there?
m:For two years. I left in 2024, when I moved here.
f:And what have you done since then?
m:I've worked part-time at a bookstore downtown.
f:Have you ever given a tour in English?
m:Yes. Last summer I led tours for a school group.
f:Great. Do you speak any other languages?
m:Portuguese and Spanish. But I've never studied French.
f:That's fine. Do you have any questions for me?
m:Yes. Are the hours flexible?

en/dialogue/db/db041615184a36de.mp3.qaTranscript: Excuse me, how much is this bag? It's 35 pounds. 3 to 5, that's expensive. But it's a very good bag. And how much are these sunglasses? They're on sale, only 15 pounds. 15 or 50? 15, 1, 5. Great, I'd like the sunglasses please. Cash for card? Card please, here you are. Thanks, enjoy your sunglasses.
en/dialogue/db/db041615184a36de.mp3.text:
f:Excuse me, how much is this bag?
m:It's thirty-five pounds.
f:Thirty-five? That's expensive!
m:But it's a very good bag.
f:And how much are these sunglasses?
m:They're on sale. Only fifteen pounds.
f:Fifteen or fifty?
m:Fifteen. One, five.
f:Great. I'd like the sunglasses, please.
m:Cash or card?
f:Card, please. Here you are.
m:Thanks! Enjoy your sunglasses!

en/dialogue/dc/dca4c38eab265788.mp3.text:
f:OK, everyone, let's begin. Tonight's topic is the traffic outside the school.
m:It's dangerous. If we don't do something soon, a child will get hurt.
f:I agree, but what exactly do you suggest?
m:I suggest we close the street to cars from eight to nine.
f:My customers won't come unless they can park near the shop.
f:That's a fair point. Is there a solution that works for everyone?
f:How about a walking bus? Volunteers walk groups of kids to school.
m:I love that idea. As long as we have enough volunteers, it'll work.
f:We could start a trial as soon as the council agrees.
f:And if fewer parents drive, there'll be more parking for my customers!
m:Exactly. I'll ask the other parents when I see them on Monday.
f:Great. I'll write to the council tomorrow, and we'll vote next month.

en/dialogue/e4/e440d080e3cfe1af.mp3.text:
f:Have you seen these new labels on the plots? They're in English, Vietnamese and Spanish. Who could be making them?
m:It can't be the council. Their signs are always printed, and these are clearly handwritten.
f:True. It might be Rosa. She speaks Spanish, and she's always talking about making newcomers feel welcome.
m:But Rosa doesn't speak Vietnamese, as far as I know. It must be someone who speaks all three.
f:Or it could be a group of people. Plenty of families around here speak two or three languages at home.
m:That's what I love about this place. When I arrived, I didn't know a soul, and now I really feel I belong.
f:You must feel completely at home by now. You're here more often than I am!
m:Almost. I'm still Polish at heart, but Melbourne has become part of who I am.
f:I think that's normal. Identity isn't fixed — it keeps changing as your life changes.
m:Wait, look over there. That teenager with the paint pens must be our mysterious sign maker.
f:That's Mr. Tran's grandson! He can't be older than fifteen, and he must be fluent in all three languages.
m:Then he deserves a thank-you card — in three languages, of course.

en/dialogue/e5/e562712d716c5a28.mp3.qaTranscript: Is this your family Jamal? Yes, this is my mom, and that's my dad. And who's the little girl? That's my sister's daughter, Sara. Oh, she's cute. How old is she? She's four. Her brother is seven. Are your grandparents in the photo? Yes, my grandmas here, on the left. Is your family big? Yes, I've got three sisters in ten cousins. Wow, my family is very small.
en/dialogue/e5/e562712d716c5a28.mp3.text:
f:Is this your family, Jamal?
m:Yes. This is my mom, and that's my dad.
f:And who's the little girl?
m:That's my sister's daughter, Zara.
f:Oh, she's cute! How old is she?
m:She's four. Her brother is seven.
f:Are your grandparents in the photo?
m:Yes, my grandma's here, on the left.
f:Is your family big?
m:Yes! I've got three sisters and ten cousins.
f:Wow! My family's very small.

en/dialogue/ea/ea228f90f0efd1da.mp3.qaTranscript: So what does your cousin look like? Well, he's tall and very young. Has he got short hair? No, he's got long curly hair. Is he the man with the glasses? No, deaf hasn't got glasses. What about the man with a beard? Yes, that's deaf. He's got a beard now. He looks friendly. He is, and he's very funny. Tom, hi, and your Priya, right?
en/dialogue/ea/ea228f90f0efd1da.mp3.text:
f:So, what does your cousin look like?
m:Well, he's tall and very young.
f:Has he got short hair?
m:No, he's got long curly hair.
f:Is he the man with the glasses?
m:No, Dev hasn't got glasses.
f:What about the man with the beard?
m:Yes, that's Dev! He's got a beard now!
f:He looks friendly.
m:He is. And he's very funny.
m:Tom! Hi! And you're Priya, right?

en/dialogue/ea/ea4d1061a237d528.mp3.text:
m:OK, it's movie night. What are we watching?
f:How about "The Quiet Year"? It's the one that won the big prize at the festival last month.
m:Isn't that the really long drama about a farmer?
f:It's two hours and forty minutes, actually. It's about a farmer in Iceland who stops speaking after his wife leaves him.
m:That sounds a bit depressing for a Friday night.
f:The reviews say it's beautiful. The director, who also wrote the script, spent five years making it.
m:I'm sure it's brilliant, but I'm exhausted. I want something light. What about "Double Booking"?
f:The comedy about the two wedding planners? My sister saw it. She said the plot was really predictable.
m:Predictable is fine! I don't want to think tonight.
f:You always say that. The last time we watched a comedy, you fell asleep after twenty minutes.
m:That was because it was boring, not because I was tired!
f:Hmm. What else is on? Oh, "Night Signal", the new thriller, is available too. It's set on a space station.
m:Is that the one with Lara Quinn, whose last film was terrible?
f:She's actually really good in this one. Jonas watched it on Wednesday, and he told me he couldn't sleep afterwards.
m:Then definitely not! I need to sleep tonight.
f:OK, so no drama and no thriller. Fine, we'll watch your comedy. But I'm choosing the snacks.
m:Deal. And next Friday, we'll watch your farmer movie. I promise.
f:You said that last week about the documentary!
m:That's true. OK, I'll put it in the calendar right now. Happy?
f:Very.

en/dialogue/ea/eab4cfa4dab40c93.mp3.text:
m:Good morning, Harbor Property Management. Luke speaking.
f:Hi. Could I speak to Mr. Kowalski, please?
m:I'm sorry, he's in a meeting. Can I take a message?
f:Yes, please. This is Sophie Martin from apartment 12.
f:I'm calling about my heater. It doesn't work.
m:OK. Could you spell your last name, please?
f:M-A-R-T-I-N. Could you ask him to call me back?
m:Of course. What's the best number for you?
f:It's 555-0147. I'm home all afternoon.
m:Great. He's free at two, so I can give him the message then.
f:Thanks. And could you tell him that it's really cold?
m:Sure, I can tell him. Have a good day!

en/dialogue/ee/ee18f9299be3dfdb.mp3.qaTranscript: Hi, Ruth, are you free on Saturday? Not in the morning. I work on Saturdays. How about Saturday afternoon? Yes, I'm free then. What do you want to do? Let's go to the beach. Um, I don't really like the beach. Okay. How about going to the movies? Maybe. Why don't we have a picnic in the park? Good idea. I love picnics. Let's meet at the park cafe at two. Perfect, can I bring my sister, Tess? Of course, see you on Saturday.
en/dialogue/ee/ee18f9299be3dfdb.mp3.text:
m:Hi, Ruth! Are you free on Saturday?
f:Not in the morning. I work on Saturdays.
m:How about Saturday afternoon?
f:Yes, I'm free then. What do you want to do?
m:Let's go to the beach!
f:Hmm, I don't really like the beach.
m:OK. How about going to the movies?
f:Maybe. Why don't we have a picnic in the park?
m:Good idea! I love picnics.
f:Let's meet at the park café at two.
m:Perfect. Can I bring my sister, Tess?
f:Of course! See you on Saturday!

en/dialogue/f0/f00ce1a3092ce209.mp3.qaTranscript: Any plans for the weekend, a chat? Yes, I'm going to go camping. Camping, where? In the mountains, with my brother and his kids. Great, is it going to be cold? Maybe, but we've got warm sweaters, and you. Nothing special, I'm going to sleep late. Are you going to see your friends? Yes, we're going to have a barbecue on Sunday. Sounds fun, have a great weekend. You too, take a lot of photos.
en/dialogue/f0/f00ce1a3092ce209.mp3.text:
m:Any plans for the weekend, Asha?
f:Yes! I'm going to go camping.
m:Camping? Where?
f:In the mountains, with my brother and his kids.
m:Great! Is it going to be cold?
f:Maybe, but we've got warm sweaters. And you?
m:Nothing special. I'm going to sleep late.
f:Are you going to see your friends?
m:Yes, we're going to have a barbecue on Sunday.
f:Sounds fun! Have a great weekend!
m:You too! Take a lot of photos!

en/dialogue/f3/f33084f2fee4ab5d.mp3.qaTranscript: Hi. Bruno, what are you doing? Hi, Lucy. I'm watching a movie at home. It's raining here. Is it raining there? Yes, it's raining and it's very windy. Are you free on Saturday? Yes, I am. Why? Let's go to the beach. But the weather is terrible. Not on Saturday. It's going to be sunny and hot. Really? Okay. Why not? Great. Do you want to take a picnic? Good idea, I love picnics, I can make sandwiches. And I can bring some fruit and drinks. What time? How about 10 o 'clock at the bus stop? Perfect, see you on Saturday.
en/dialogue/f3/f33084f2fee4ab5d.mp3.text:
f:Hi, Bruno! What are you doing?
m:Hi, Lucy. I'm watching a movie at home.
f:It's raining here. Is it raining there?
m:Yes, it's raining and it's very windy.
f:Are you free on Saturday?
m:Yes, I am. Why?
f:Let's go to the beach!
m:But the weather is terrible!
f:Not on Saturday. It's going to be sunny and hot.
m:Really? OK, why not?
f:Great. Do you want to take a picnic?
m:Good idea. I love picnics. I can make sandwiches.
f:And I can bring some fruit and drinks.
m:What time?
f:How about ten o'clock at the bus stop?
m:Perfect. See you on Saturday!

en/dialogue/f7/f7210b754c55d9c0.mp3.text:
f:This stream used to be buried under a busy elevated highway. It was taken down in the early two thousands.
m:Really? Removing a highway in the middle of a city must have caused chaos.
f:Many people expected it to. But owing to big improvements in the bus network, the traffic was more manageable than they'd feared.
m:So drivers switched to public transport instead of simply driving somewhere else?
f:Many did. Buses became faster and more reliable, which is why a lot of commuters left their cars at home.
m:And now the place is full of people. It feels so calm that it's hard to believe we're downtown.
f:Exactly. As a result of the restoration, the area around the stream is also noticeably cooler in summer.
m:Is that because of the water itself, or because there's less concrete?
f:Both, apparently. The water and the trees absorb heat, whereas roads and buildings store it.
