en/dialogue/f8/f85645163c74a000.mp3.text:
f:This week, one headline caught a lot of attention: "Late starts make teenagers smarter." Rahul, is that what the research actually shows?
m:Not quite. Headlines like that tend to exaggerate. What has been found, in a number of studies, is that when schools start later, teenagers get more sleep — in some cases around half an hour more each night.
f:Why does that matter so much for teenagers in particular?
m:During adolescence, the body clock shifts. Teenagers are biologically programmed to fall asleep later, so asking them to be in class at eight is a bit like asking adults to start work at six.
f:And the "smarter" part of the headline?
m:Some studies have reported better attendance and slightly better grades after start times were moved. But it's difficult to prove that sleep alone caused the improvement. Other changes may have been introduced at the same time.
f:So the claim isn't false, but it's oversimplified?
m:Exactly. "Smarter" is the wrong word. "Better rested" would be more accurate.
f:How much sleep do teenagers actually need?
m:Most guidelines recommend between eight and ten hours a night. Many teenagers get far less than that on school nights and then try to catch up at weekends, which doesn't fully make up for it.
f:Several listeners have asked how scientists actually measure sleep in studies like these.
m:Often, students wear a small device on their wrist that records movement. In more detailed studies, participants have their brain activity monitored overnight in a sleep lab.
f:Are there any downsides to later starts?
m:There can be practical ones. Buses have to be rescheduled, after-school sports finish later, and parents' working hours don't always fit. Those problems are real, and they've been the main reason why some schools haven't made the change.
f:If a parent is listening and is worried about their teenager's sleep, what would you suggest?
m:Keep phones out of the bedroom at night if possible, and keep wake-up times fairly regular, even at weekends. Getting some daylight in the morning helps the body clock, too. And if a teenager is exhausted despite sleeping enough, it's worth getting them checked by a doctor.
f:Rahul Menon, thank you very much.
m:Thanks for having me.

en/dialogue/fc/fc63a2ff832463bd.mp3.text:
f:Dev! You did it! How does it feel to have survived your first open-mic night?
m:Terrifying. I did warn you it would be a disaster. Did you hear the silence after my first joke?
f:Such was the silence that I could hear the bartender drying glasses.
m:Thanks. Very supportive. Now be honest — did anybody actually laugh?
f:People did laugh at the pun about the dentist. "Looking down in the mouth" — I loved that one.
m:That's the one I almost cut! So nervous was I before the show that I nearly cut half my set.
f:The problem wasn't the jokes, though. You do tend to rush the punchlines when you're nervous.
m:I know. And the sarcastic bit about my landlord just sounded mean.
f:Sarcasm is tricky. Self-deprecating jokes work much better — people love it when you laugh at yourself.
m:Like the story about my driving test? That did get the biggest laugh of the night.
f:Exactly. And so well did it go that the host asked whether you'd come back next month.
m:Seriously? Then I'd better start writing. And this time I'll slow down — I really will.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/02/02413d2178e7b.text: Think about the last time you did absolutely nothing. Not scrolling through your phone, not listening to a podcast, not "relaxing" with a TV series — just sitting, looking out of a window and letting your mind wander. For many of us, it's hard to remember. We live in a culture that celebrates being busy. People who are always rushing are often seen as successful, and free time is something that we try to fill. Even our hobbies have become goals: the run that has to be faster, the reading list that has to be longer. But some psychologists believe that the moments when we do nothing are exactly the moments that we need most. When your brain isn't focused on a task, it doesn't switch off. Instead, it starts making connections between ideas, memories and experiences. This is why so many people get their best ideas in the shower, on a walk or just before they fall asleep. A mind that is allowed to wander is often a mind that solves problems. Doing nothing can also help us recover from stress. People who take short breaks without screens during the day often say that they feel calmer and concentrate better afterwards. Some studies suggest that even a few minutes of quiet can improve your mood. Of course, doing nothing is harder than it sounds. The first few minutes can feel uncomfortable, even boring. That's completely normal. If you want to try, choose a place where you won't be disturbed — a park bench, a balcony or a quiet corner of your home. Leave your phone in another room. Start with five minutes, and slowly make it longer. Don't judge the thoughts that come into your head; just notice them. The Dutch even have a word for it: niksen, which means doing nothing on purpose. So the next time someone asks what you did at the weekend, try answering, "Nothing at all." Then smile. You might be the most productive person in the room.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/08/084092ef876a1.text: For more than four hundred years, the women of Santa Lúcia, a small village in the mountains of northern Portugal, wove blankets in a pattern found nowhere else in the world. Each blanket took months to complete, and the designs, which were never written down, were passed from mother to daughter. By the early twenty-tens, however, only three weavers were still working, and the youngest of them was seventy-eight. Rarely does a tradition disappear overnight. In Santa Lúcia, it faded slowly, as young people left for jobs in the cities and cheap factory-made blankets filled the markets. "Nobody thought of it as heritage," says Rita Fonseca, who grew up in the village. "It was just something our grandmothers did. Only when my grandmother became ill did I realize that the patterns would die with her." Fonseca, then a twenty-six-year-old graphic designer, moved back to the village and asked the three remaining weavers to teach her. Little did she know that she would spend the next two years learning a single pattern. "Not only were the techniques incredibly complex," she says, "but the weavers themselves had never had to explain them. They just knew." No sooner had she posted photos of her first blanket online than messages began to arrive from all over the world. Designers wanted to collaborate, museums asked to borrow pieces, and — most importantly — young people from the region asked to learn. Today, the village workshop has fourteen apprentices, and the patterns have finally been recorded, stitch by stitch, in a digital archive. Not everyone is enthusiastic. Some older residents worry that the blankets are becoming expensive souvenirs for tourists instead of objects for everyday use. Others feel uncomfortable seeing their family designs printed on cushions sold in city boutiques. Under no circumstances, the workshop insists, will the original patterns be sold to factories, and every blanket is still made entirely by hand. The debate reflects a question faced by heritage projects everywhere: how can a tradition be protected without being frozen in time? Seldom is the answer simple. A craft that never changes may survive only in museums, while one that changes too much may lose what made it special. For Fonseca, the answer lies in people rather than objects. "A blanket in a glass case is beautiful," she says. "But a tradition is only alive while someone is still learning it." In Santa Lúcia, at least for now, someone is.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/10/10eb1c7278752.text: This month's guest at the Riverside Library Book Club is Rosa Delgado, whose first novel, The Night Ferry, has been on the bestseller list for twelve weeks. Before she became a writer, Rosa spent fifteen years as a singer-songwriter. She grew up in San Antonio, Texas, where her parents ran a small record store, and she started writing songs at thirteen. Her first album, which she recorded in her bedroom, sold only two hundred copies. "My mom bought fifty of them," she jokes. For years she toured small clubs and cafés across the US with her band, which made very little money but had a loyal group of fans. Then, in 2021, she lost her voice for six months because of a throat problem, which was a disaster for a singer. "I couldn't sing, so I started writing stories instead," she says. "It turned out to be the best thing that ever happened to me." The Night Ferry tells the story of Lola, a young musician who travels to Ireland to find her missing father. Most of the novel takes place on a ferry between Wales and Dublin during a single stormy night. The book, which Rosa wrote in just nine months, is full of music: every chapter starts with a line from a song, and Rosa has recorded an album of the songs, which readers can listen to online. Rosa now lives in Austin with her partner, Jo, who is a drummer, and their two cats, which are named after famous jazz singers. She still sings, but only at home. "My cats are my toughest critics," she says. Join us on Thursday, May 14, at 7 p.m. in the main reading room. Rosa will read from the novel, answer your questions and, if her voice allows it, sing one song.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/11/11ca60e804768.text: Good evening, everyone. I'd like to begin with a simple question: how old will you be in twenty-five years? For many of us in this room, the answer is "over seventy." And we won't be alone. Worldwide, the number of people aged eighty or over is expected to roughly triple by twenty-fifty. In our own city, one in four residents is set to be over sixty-five within the next two decades. Tonight, I want to make the case that we need to start designing our streets, homes and services for that future now — not when it arrives. Let me give you three reasons. Firstly, it is cheaper. Building a step-free station costs far less than rebuilding an old one later. Our new tram line is due to open in two years, and it is about to enter its final design stage. If we add level boarding, benches and clear signs now, the extra cost is small. If we wait, it is bound to be much higher. Secondly, a city that works for older people works for everyone. Wider sidewalks help parents with strollers. Public restrooms help delivery drivers and tourists. Benches every few hundred meters help anyone carrying heavy shopping. Designing for age is not a favor to one group; it is simply good design. Thirdly, loneliness. Many older residents tell us that they stop going out not because they are unwell, but because the journey has become stressful: busy crossings, broken sidewalks, nowhere to rest. When people stop going out, they lose contact with friends and neighbors, and their health is likely to get worse. Small changes can keep people connected for years longer. Now, some of you may be thinking: with so many pressing problems, is this really a priority? It's a fair question. Our budget is limited, and housing and climate are urgent issues too. But these goals are not in competition. A walkable neighborhood with local shops, parks and good public transport is greener, healthier and better for every generation. So what am I asking for? Three things. First, that every new public project includes an age-friendly checklist. Second, that residents over seventy are invited to test new designs before they are built. And third, that the council commits to reviewing progress every two years. To sum up: we are on the verge of a historic change in the age of our population. We can see it coming, which means we can prepare for it. In twenty-five years' time, I hope we will look back and say that we planned well — for our parents, for ourselves and for our children. Thank you.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/1e/1e53ae71d4bb8.text: When people find out that I grew up speaking Portuguese at home and English at school, they tend to ask the same question: "Which language do you dream in?" The honest answer is that I'm not sure. I seem to dream in whichever language the people in the dream speak, which is probably the least exciting answer possible. A more interesting question, I'd say, is whether I'm the same person in both languages. My friends would argue that I'm not. In English, I apparently come across as fairly reserved and rather precise; I choose my words carefully and rarely interrupt. In Portuguese, I talk faster, laugh louder and use my hands far more. My mother, who is arguably the best judge, says I'm warmer in Portuguese and more efficient in English. I'm still not sure which one is the compliment. I used to think this was evidence that I had two personalities. Now I suspect it's something more ordinary. Each language came with its own context: Portuguese was the language of family dinners, arguments and jokes, while English was the language of classrooms, exams and, later, job interviews. It's likely that I'm simply carrying those settings with me. Many bilingual people describe something similar, and some researchers have suggested that the situations in which we learn a language may shape how we behave when we use it. Living between languages isn't always comfortable. There are things I can only talk about in one of them. I can explain a mortgage in English but not in Portuguese, and I can describe my grandmother's cooking properly only in Portuguese. When I'm tired, I tend to switch between the two in the middle of a sentence, which my colleagues find slightly confusing. And there is the occasional feeling of being a little foreign everywhere: a bit too American for my cousins in Porto, and a bit too Portuguese for my neighbors in Boston. Still, I wouldn't change it. Having two languages is rather like having two windows in the same room. The view from each one is somewhat different, but it's the same room. If anything, moving between them has taught me that there is rarely only one way to say something — or to be someone.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/1f/1f0c71ae96b24.text: Every year, paintings worth millions are sold, exhibited and admired — and some of them are fakes. Experts disagree about how many, but few doubt that forgeries hang in respected collections around the world. How, then, are they found? The first line of defense is provenance: the documented history of a work's ownership. A genuine painting usually leaves a trail of sales receipts, exhibition catalogs, letters and photographs. Gaps in that trail are not proof of forgery — records are lost in wars, fires and house moves — but they make experts cautious. Clever forgers know this, which is why some have gone as far as inventing entire histories, complete with fake labels on the back of the canvas. The second line is the expert eye. Specialists who have spent decades studying a single artist learn to recognize the way that artist painted a hand, built up a shadow or signed a name. Rarely can a forger imitate every habit at once. Yet the eye can be fooled. Some famous forgeries of the twentieth century were accepted as genuine by leading experts, partly because the experts wanted them to be real. That is why, increasingly, the final word belongs to science. Viewed under ultraviolet light, areas of later retouching often appear darker than the original paint, revealing repairs or additions. X-rays can show what lies beneath the surface: an earlier composition, a change of mind or, in some cases, a completely different painting, reused by a forger to obtain an old canvas. Chemical analysis of pigments is particularly powerful, because many pigments have known dates of invention. Titanium white, for example, did not become widely available as an artists' paint until the twentieth century. Found in a painting supposedly made in the sixteen hundreds, it is a clear sign that something is wrong — unless it belongs to a later restoration. For paintings on wooden panels, the growth rings of the wood can be compared with historical records to estimate when the tree was cut down. And radiocarbon dating can show whether a canvas was made after the middle of the twentieth century, when nuclear weapons tests changed the amount of a particular form of carbon in the atmosphere. Not only are these methods becoming more accurate, but they are also becoming cheaper and less destructive, often needing a sample smaller than a grain of sand. Even so, science has its limits. A test can prove that a painting is not what it claims to be, but it can rarely prove beyond doubt that a work is genuine. A skilled forger using old materials may pass every test. In the end, authenticating a painting is a little like solving a crime: no single clue is enough, but together, documents, expert judgment and laboratory evidence can build a convincing case. And the stakes are high. No collector who has paid a fortune for a masterpiece wants to discover that it was painted last year.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/31/31f645922c2ea.text: When I was fourteen, my best friend was a girl called Nadia. We used to walk to school together every morning, and we would spend every weekend at her house, where her mother made the best cheese pies in the neighborhood. We shared everything: clothes, secrets, even a bike. Then, in our last year of high school, we fell out. It started with something small. Nadia had won a place at a university in another city, and I hadn't. Instead of congratulating her, I said something unkind — I can't even remember exactly what. She looked at me for a long moment, picked up her bag and left. We didn't speak for eleven years. For a long time, I told myself that it was her fault. She was stubborn, I thought, and she never forgave anyone. But the truth was simpler and more uncomfortable: I was jealous, and I was too proud to apologize. Last spring, I was waiting for a train in Chicago when I heard someone laugh behind me. I knew that laugh immediately. I turned around, and there she was, holding a coffee and a very large suitcase. For a second, neither of us said anything. Then she smiled and said, "You still have that terrible green scarf." We both missed our trains. We sat in the station café for three hours and talked about everything that had happened since school: jobs, moves, her two children, my divorce, her mother's illness. At one point, I finally apologized. "I'm sorry about what I said," I told her. "I was jealous." She shook her head. "I was angry for about a week," she said. "After that, I just missed you." Now we talk every Sunday. We live in different states, but we're as close as we used to be — maybe closer. I've learned two things from Nadia. First, an argument doesn't have to be the end of a friendship. And second, never wait eleven years to say sorry.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/5f/5f3b4d01974d3.text: Six months ago, Fernhill Design, a small marketing agency in Leeds with twenty-two employees, made a bold decision: everyone would work four days a week, for the same salary. Since January, the office has been closed on Fridays. "At first, I was worried," says the company's founder, Grace Mensah. "Our clients expect fast answers, and I thought we would lose business." To prepare, the team changed the way they work. Meetings now last a maximum of thirty minutes, and staff check their emails only three times a day. In addition, every Monday the team agrees on a short list of priorities for the week. The results have surprised everyone. Although the team works one day less, they have completed more projects than in the same period last year. Sick days have fallen by almost half. "I've been sleeping much better since we started," says designer Tom Halloran. "On Fridays I do the shopping and the cleaning, so the weekend is really free. As a result, I come back on Monday with a lot more energy." However, the change hasn't been easy for everyone. Some clients complained at first that nobody answered the phone on Fridays, so now one person is on call each week. A few employees also say that the four working days feel more intense. "There's no time to chat with colleagues anymore," says account manager Priya Das. "I miss that." Fernhill isn't alone. Companies in several countries have been testing shorter working weeks, and many of them have decided to keep them. Experts say that a four-day week doesn't work for every job — hospitals, schools and stores need staff every day — but for many office jobs, it can be a real option. For Grace Mensah, the decision is now easy. "We're keeping it," she says. "Our team is happier, and our clients are happy too. Honestly, I can't imagine going back."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/5f/5fcab6eb1eabd.text: Last month, my grandmother Gloria turned eighty, and our whole family had a big party for her. At the party, I asked her about her life. Here is her story. Gloria was born in 1946 in a small village in Trinidad. Her parents were farmers, and she had four brothers. She didn't have many toys when she was a child, but she loved school, and she walked five kilometers there every day. When she was nineteen, she got a job as a nurse in Port of Spain, the capital. Then, in 1968, she saw an ad for nurses in Toronto, and she decided to go. "I was scared," she told me. "I didn't know anyone, and I didn't have a winter coat!" Her first winter in Canada was very hard. It snowed in October, and she stayed inside on her days off. But then she met my grandfather, Henry, at the hospital. He was a doctor from Jamaica. They got married in 1971 and had three children. My mother was their third child. Gloria worked as a nurse for thirty-five years, and she retired in 2006. Now she lives in a small apartment near us. She still cooks for the family every Sunday, and she still doesn't like winter! At the end of the party, I asked her, "Did you ever want to go back?" She smiled. "Sometimes. But my family is here. This is home now."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/63/63bec13346717.text: Last month, my ten-year-old daughter came home from school convinced that a famous singer had died. She had seen it on a video app, along with thousands of sad comments. The singer, as it turned out, was alive and well and about to start a world tour. My daughter was embarrassed; I was worried. If a fake story could fool a bright ten-year-old so easily, what chance would she have against the far more sophisticated misinformation she will meet as an adult? I believe the answer is simple: media literacy should be a compulsory subject in every primary school, taught as seriously as reading and math. Some will argue that this is a job for parents, not teachers. It is true that families play an important role, and I am not suggesting that parents should step back. However, most parents were never taught these skills themselves, and many admit that they struggle to tell a reliable source from an unreliable one. Leaving it to families means leaving it to chance. Others claim that the timetable is already overcrowded. Admittedly, this is a fair point, and teachers are right to be wary of yet another subject. But media literacy does not need to replace anything. It can be built into lessons that already exist: comparing two accounts of the same event in history, checking the data behind a graph in science, or analyzing the language of advertisements in English. What it needs is time, training and a clear place in the curriculum. A third objection is that children are simply too young. Yet many ten-year-olds are already online for several hours a day. Critics who maintain that we should wait until secondary school are, in effect, arguing that we should wait until the habits are formed. As several educational researchers have pointed out, it is far easier to build good habits than to break bad ones. Of course, the aim is not to make children cynical. A child who believes nothing is as easy to manipulate as a child who believes everything. The aim is to teach them to ask a few simple questions every time they read something: Who made this? Why? How do they know? What is missing? These questions sound basic, but adults who ask them regularly are much harder to fool. No program is perfect, and the details will need careful thought. But the principle is clear. We teach children to look both ways before they cross the road — not because every car is dangerous, but because some are. It is time we taught them to look both ways before they share.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/63/63c3feb6d8ad5.text: At ten o'clock at night, when most people in Montreal are going to bed, Teresa Nwosu is starting her working day. Teresa is a baker, and she has worked the night shift at a busy bakery downtown for six years. Teresa didn't plan to be a baker. She studied chemistry at college and graduated in 2015. After college, she worked in a laboratory for three years. "The job was OK, but I didn't love it," she says. "I've always loved cooking, so I took a baking course in the evenings. On the first day, I knew this was my job!" Now Teresa is in charge of a team of four bakers. Every night, they make more than two thousand croissants, a thousand loaves of bread and hundreds of cakes. Her shift ends at six in the morning, when the first customers arrive. Has she ever wanted to change to a day job? "Never," she laughs. "The bakery is quiet at night, and my team is great. We've worked together since the bakery opened, so we're like a family." There are some problems, of course. Teresa sleeps from eight in the morning until three in the afternoon, and she has missed a lot of parties and family dinners. "My friends have learned to have lunch with me, not dinner!" she says. Her advice for young people? "Your first job doesn't have to be your last job. If you really love something, try it."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/8a/8ad46759bed1e.text: When Dolores Brennan retired from her job as a bus driver in Boston, she decided to do something that surprised her whole family: she started learning Korean. She was sixty-nine. "My granddaughter had married a wonderful man from Busan," she explains, "and I wanted to talk to his parents without needing an interpreter at every family dinner." At first, it wasn't easy. Dolores had never studied a foreign language, and she found the new alphabet terrifying. "I kept mixing up the letters. After two weeks, I almost gave up." Then her teacher at the community center gave her some advice that she still remembers: "Stop trying to be perfect. Try to be curious." Dolores changed her approach. Instead of memorizing long lists of words, she started watching Korean cooking shows, which helped her pick up everyday vocabulary. She also began writing a short diary in Korean every evening — just three or four sentences about her day. "Nobody reads it, so I'm allowed to make as many mistakes as I want," she laughs. Three years later, she can hold a simple conversation, read restaurant menus and, most importantly, chat with her granddaughter's in-laws on video calls. Last spring, she traveled to Busan and spent two weeks with them. "We cooked together every day, and I didn't need anyone to translate a single recipe," she says proudly. Research suggests that older learners often have some advantages. They are usually good at organizing their study time, and they know how they learn best. What they sometimes lack is confidence. So what is Dolores's advice for people who want to start a language later in life? "You don't have to be young, and you don't have to be talented. You just have to keep going. And you should choose something you love — food, music, family. That's what keeps you going on the difficult days."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/8f/8f37aa7840e41.text: Ask Leila Haddad where she is from, and she will smile and ask how much time you have. Born in Beirut to a Lebanese father and a Danish mother, she spent her childhood in Nairobi, her teenage years in Singapore and her twenties in Toronto, where she now works as a school counselor. "When people ask where home is," she says, "I usually say 'wherever my books are.'" Leila is what researchers call a third culture kid: someone who spent a significant part of their childhood outside their parents' culture. The term was first used by American sociologists in the nineteen fifties to describe the children of diplomats, missionaries and military families. Today, with millions of families moving abroad for work, the group is far larger and far more varied. Third culture kids tend to share certain strengths. Having moved so often, many are remarkably adaptable. They are often multilingual, quick to notice cultural differences and comfortable with people from very different backgrounds. International employers frequently value exactly these skills. But the experience also has a cost, and it can take years to recognize it. Many adults who grew up this way describe a feeling of rootlessness: they seem to belong everywhere and nowhere. Leila remembers returning to Lebanon at eighteen, expecting to feel at home, only to find that her cousins considered her a foreigner. "My Arabic was fine, but I didn't know the songs, the jokes or the TV shows," she says. "I must have looked Lebanese, but I certainly didn't sound it." Another common experience is unresolved grief. Every move means saying goodbye — to friends, to schools, to a favorite café or the view from a bedroom window. Because these losses are rarely seen as serious, children are seldom given time to mourn them. Some researchers suggest that this may explain why many third culture kids find it hard to form deep friendships as adults: if you expect to leave, it can seem safer not to get too close. The good news is that awareness has grown considerably. International schools increasingly run "leaving programs" that help children say goodbye properly, and online communities connect adults who share the same background. For many, simply discovering that there is a name for their experience is a relief. In her work, Leila now helps students through the same transitions she once went through. Her advice to parents is practical. "Don't promise that the next place will feel just like home — it won't. Let your children be sad about what they're leaving. And give them something that travels with them: a tradition, a language, a family ritual. Roots don't have to be in the ground. They can be in the things you do together." Asked whether she would raise her own children the same way, she pauses. "Probably, yes," she says. "I might move less often. But I wouldn't give up what it taught me — that there are many ways to be at home in the world."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/98/9819f3e6755d9.text: Before I moved from Bristol to Helsinki for work three years ago, everyone gave me the same warning: "Finns don't talk." My friends imagined that I would spend my winters in total silence, surrounded by people who never smiled. The reality was more interesting. It's true that many Finns don't enjoy small talk. People rarely chat with strangers at the bus stop, and in my first few months I found the silence in the office kitchen almost painful. Back home, a quiet moment is something you fill — with a comment about the weather, a joke, anything. Here, silence is comfortable. People speak when they have something to say. Once I understood that, I started to like it. My Finnish colleagues are warm, funny and incredibly honest. When they invite you to their home, they mean it. And when they say, "Let's have coffee sometime," they actually put it in the calendar! Some customs took longer to learn. You always take your shoes off when you go into someone's home, and you should be punctual — five minutes late is late. The sauna isn't just a place to relax; it's where friends, families and even colleagues have some of their best conversations. Of course, stereotypes work both ways. My neighbors were sure that I drank tea all day and talked about the weather constantly. To be fair, they weren't completely wrong. Do I have any regrets? Only a few. I wish I spoke better Finnish — it's a beautiful but very difficult language, and I still can't follow conversations at parties. I wish I could explain to people back home that "quiet" doesn't mean "cold." And on dark January afternoons, I sometimes wish the sun didn't set at half past three. But stereotypes are only the first page of the story. If you stay long enough, you get to read the rest.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/9c/9c335e0dcf147.text: Two years ago, my partner Dev and I left our tiny apartment in Manchester and moved to a village in the hills of north Wales. Our friends thought we were crazy. Here's what we've learned so far. The village is small — about four hundred people live here — and it is surrounded by farms and forests. Life is slower. The only shop is run by volunteers, and it's closed on Sundays. Bread is delivered from a bakery in the next town twice a week, and most of the vegetables in the shop are grown on farms nearby. Getting around is the hardest part. There are only four buses a day, so most journeys here are made by car, which isn't very green. Our waste is collected just once every two weeks, so we've learned to recycle and compost almost everything. What do we miss? Movie theaters, late-night food and being able to walk everywhere. What don't we miss? The noise, the traffic and paying half our salaries in rent. Here, the air is clean, you can see the stars at night, and everyone says hello in the street. The village hall is used for everything: yoga on Mondays, a film club on Fridays and a market once a month. People often ask us if we feel lonely. Honestly? Sometimes, especially in winter. But the community is warm, and new people are always invited to the Friday film club. Will we stay forever? We don't know. But for now, the hills feel like home.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/a4/a4a54f1ad8f18.text: Every Saturday, I have lunch at Halden Street Market, an old covered market in the city where I grew up. It's the place where I learned that food is more than something you eat. It's a story. The first stall I always visit belongs to Amara, a woman whose family came from Ghana in the 1980s. She sells jollof rice, and the recipe she uses is the one her grandmother taught her. "People argue about jollof," she told me, laughing. "Every family thinks theirs is the best." Next to her is a Polish bakery whose rye bread sells out by eleven o'clock. The baker, Tomasz, gets up at three every morning. "The bread my customers love takes eighteen hours to make," he says. "You can't hurry it." Further along, there's a small counter where two brothers make Vietnamese sandwiches called bánh mì. The bread they use comes from Tomasz's bakery — a perfect example of how the market works. Everyone here buys from everyone else. What I love most is the long table in the middle of the market, where strangers sit together and share their food. Last week I sat next to a retired teacher whose son had just opened a taco stand, and a student who was trying jollof for the first time. We talked for an hour. In a world where many of us eat lunch alone at our desks, the market reminds me of something important: the meals we remember are usually the ones we share.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/b0/b06d7ab5f97bc.text: When Jordan Ellis applied for forty jobs in two months and received forty automatic rejections, he began to suspect that no human had ever read his applications. He was probably right. A growing number of large employers now use software to screen job applications, and many candidates are rejected before a person even sees their name. Supporters of these systems argue that they make hiring faster and, potentially, fairer. A popular job advert can attract thousands of applications, and human recruiters, it is often pointed out, have biases of their own. People tend to favor candidates who remind them of themselves — who went to the same university, share the same hobbies or have similar names. An algorithm, the argument goes, does not care about any of that. The problem is that an algorithm learns from data, and data reflects the past. If a company has mostly hired one type of person over the last twenty years, a system trained on those decisions is likely to learn that this type of person is what "success" looks like. In one widely reported case, an experimental recruitment tool developed by a large technology company was found to give lower scores to applications that included the word "women's," as in "women's chess club." The tool was reportedly abandoned before it was used to make real decisions, but the case became a warning for the whole industry. Bias can also creep in through less obvious routes. Gaps in a CV, for example, may be treated as a negative signal, even though they are often caused by illness, caring for children or relatives, or unemployment during a recession. Video interviews analyzed by software raise further questions: can a machine fairly judge the facial expressions or speech of candidates with disabilities, or of people from cultures where eye contact is used differently? Regulators are beginning to respond. In some places, employers are now required to tell candidates when automated tools are being used, and independent audits of hiring software have been introduced to check for discrimination. Researchers are also developing methods to test algorithms for bias before they are put into use. Few experts believe that the answer is to ban these tools completely. Used carefully, they can help employers look beyond the usual universities and networks and find talented people who might otherwise have been overlooked. But that requires transparency: candidates should know how they are being assessed, and humans should remain responsible for the final decision. Jordan eventually found a job — through a friend who passed his CV directly to a manager. "It's ironic," he says. "Everyone talks about technology making things fairer, and in the end I got hired the old-fashioned way: because somebody knew somebody."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/b3/b3df14938be7c.text: Last October, I did something that many of my friends thought was crazy: I took the train from Toronto to Vancouver. The flight takes about five hours. The train takes four days. I'd been thinking about the trip for years. I had flown across Canada many times for work, but I had never really seen the country — just clouds and an airport at each end. So when I finally had two weeks of vacation, I booked a small sleeping cabin and packed three books, a notebook and some warm socks. The first day was all forests and lakes, thousands of them, shining in the fall sunshine. On the second day, we crossed the prairies, which were so flat and empty that I could see storms coming from hours away. In the dining car, passengers sat together at shared tables, so every meal was a conversation with strangers: a retired farmer from Saskatchewan, two students from Germany, a nurse who was going to meet her new grandson. By the third day, we were greeting each other like old friends. Then came the Rocky Mountains. I was sitting in the observation car, which had a glass roof, when the train came out of a tunnel, and suddenly there they were — huge, snowy and silent. Nobody spoke for a full minute. Was it the cheapest or the fastest choice? Definitely not. My sleeping cabin cost more than three flights, and I spent four days of my vacation on the journey. If I had to choose only on price, I'd fly. But travel isn't only about arriving. If more of us traveled slowly, I think we would see our countries — and each other — a little differently. I'm already planning my next slow journey. I just wish trains in North America were a little faster, and a lot cheaper.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/bb/bbc5c26dd6392.text: Every summer, it seems, the same images appear on the news: streets turned into rivers, cars floating in underpasses, basements full of water. As the climate warms, heavy rainstorms are becoming more frequent and more intense in many parts of the world. Yet the cities hit hardest are often not the ones with the most rain, but the ones with the most concrete. The reason is simple. In a natural landscape, much of the rain that falls soaks into the ground, where it is absorbed by soil and plants. In a modern city, by contrast, roads, roofs and parking lots are almost entirely waterproof. As a result, rainwater has nowhere to go except into drains, and when the drains are overwhelmed, it floods the streets. For most of the twentieth century, the solution was to build bigger pipes and higher walls. The idea behind the "sponge city" is the opposite: instead of moving water away as fast as possible, cities should hold on to it, slow it down and let it soak in. The term became widely known after China launched a national program in twenty-fifteen, but similar ideas have been used in cities from Copenhagen to Melbourne. What does a sponge city look like? It might include parks designed to flood safely, turning into temporary lakes during a storm and drying out afterward. It might involve green roofs covered in plants, which absorb rain and keep buildings cooler. Sidewalks can be made of permeable materials that let water pass through, and streets can be lined with planted channels, sometimes called rain gardens, that collect the runoff from the road. The benefits go beyond flood protection. Because the water is stored rather than wasted, it can be used to water parks during dry periods. Plants and open water cool the air, which matters in cities that are getting hotter. And many residents simply enjoy living near more green space. There are limitations, though. Sponge features work well for frequent, moderate storms, but they cannot absorb the most extreme downpours on their own, so traditional drainage is still needed. Retrofitting existing neighborhoods is expensive and disruptive, and green infrastructure needs regular maintenance, which is often underfunded once the ribbon has been cut. Critics also point out that some projects have been more about appearance than performance. Despite these challenges, many planners believe that the approach represents a fundamental change in thinking. For a century, cities treated rain as waste to be removed as quickly as possible. Now, many are learning to treat it as a resource. Whether they can make that change quickly enough is another question.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/c6/c6cf59600cd2f.text: MILLBROOK, Vermont — Staff at Millbrook Public Library got a surprise on Monday morning when a small package arrived from Spain. Inside the package were a 1960s travel guide to Europe, a handwritten letter and a check for $100. The book had been missing since 1974. The letter came from Margaret Ellis, 73, who grew up in Millbrook. She explained that she had borrowed the book in the summer of 1974, just before she left for a year of study in Madrid. "I had planned to return it when I came back," she wrote, "but I fell in love with the city, and I never came home." Ms. Ellis found the book last month while she was clearing out her attic. "As soon as I saw the library stamp, I felt terrible," she said in a phone interview. "I'd carried that book across an ocean and through fifty years of my life, and I had completely forgotten that it wasn't mine." Librarian Tom Becker said that nothing like this had ever happened in his thirty years at the library. "By the time I finished reading the letter, my whole team had gathered around my desk," he said. "Everyone was smiling." The library had stopped charging late fees in 2021, so Ms. Ellis did not owe any money. Mr. Becker said the library would use her $100 to buy new travel books. The old guide, with Ms. Ellis's notes still in the margins, now sits in a glass case near the front door.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/c9/c94655b38da7f.text: When I was eleven, my family moved from Porto, in Portugal, to Toronto. I still remember my first week at my new school, because almost everything was different. At my school in Porto, we had to stand up when a teacher came into the classroom, and we weren't allowed to call teachers by their first names. We didn't have to wear a uniform, but we couldn't wear caps inside the building. Lunch was a hot meal in the school cafeteria, and the lunch break felt long and relaxed. In Toronto, the rules were different. We didn't have to stand up, and two of my teachers asked us to call them by their first names, which felt very strange to me. On the other hand, most students brought lunch from home, and we had only forty minutes to eat it. Phones had to stay in our lockers until the end of the day, and if you broke that rule, you got a detention. The biggest surprise was the homework. In Porto, we had homework every night, and we often had to learn long lists of facts by heart. In Toronto, we had to work in groups on projects that lasted several weeks. We were allowed to use the internet, and the teachers wanted to hear our opinions, not just the right answers. At first, I hated speaking in front of the class. Now I think it was the best thing that ever happened to me. Today I'm a teacher myself, and there's a sign on my classroom door: "You must be kind. You don't have to be perfect."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/d6/d652304f53dee.text: For most of the year, Linden Street looks like any other street: parked cars on both sides, a few trees and a lot of traffic at school time. But every Sunday from May to September, something unusual happens. At eight in the morning, the street is closed to cars, and by ten it is full of children on bikes, neighbors drinking coffee on folding chairs and an old piano that is pushed out of someone's garage. The idea was proposed in 2022 by Marisol Vega, a teacher who has lived on the street for twenty years. "Our kids were growing up without ever playing outside," she says. "I thought, if we close the street for just one day a week, maybe people will come out of their houses." She collected signatures from almost every home, and the plan was approved by the city council the following spring. Not everyone was enthusiastic. Some residents were worried that they wouldn't be able to use their cars, and the owners of a café on the corner said they would lose customers. To solve these problems, a few changes were made. Residents who need to drive are allowed to leave slowly, with a volunteer walking in front of the car, and the closed section now ends before the café. Three summers later, the results are clear. According to a survey, most residents now know at least ten neighbors by name, compared with three before. The corner café, which was against the plan at first, now has its busiest day on Sundays. And last year, the idea was copied by four other streets in the city. "It isn't a revolution," Marisol says. "It's just a street. But when people slow down and say hello, a neighborhood changes." The council has promised that the program will continue as long as residents support it. Next year, the organizers hope to add a monthly repair stall and a book exchange — if they find enough volunteers.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/dc/dc4086c05ac42.text: Thousands of people in Bristol have had their blood pressure checked in libraries, community centers and even barbershops over the past year, as part of a pilot scheme designed to catch serious health problems before they become emergencies. The project, which was launched last spring by a group of local GP practices, allows anyone over forty to walk in without an appointment and have a range of basic tests done in about fifteen minutes. Visitors can get their blood pressure measured and their heart rhythm checked, and they receive advice on diet and exercise from trained health workers. According to the scheme's organizers, almost one in five of the people tested had high blood pressure that had never been diagnosed. "High blood pressure rarely causes symptoms, so many people simply don't know they have it," explained Dr. Amara Okoye, one of the GPs behind the project. "It's very treatable, but if it isn't detected, it can lead to strokes and heart attacks. Early detection really does save lives." Many of those who took part said they would not have gone to a doctor otherwise. Winston Clarke, a fifty-eight-year-old bus driver, had his blood pressure taken while he was waiting for a haircut. "I hadn't had a check-up for about ten years," he said. "They told me my reading was dangerously high, and I was referred to my GP the same week. Now I'm on medication, and I've cut down on salt. My barber probably saved my life." The scheme has not been without its critics. Some doctors have warned that walk-in tests could cause unnecessary worry, or lead to longer waiting lists if large numbers of people are referred for further tests. Others argue that the money would be better spent on reducing waiting times for existing patients. Dr. Okoye accepts that the scheme must be carefully evaluated. "We need to make sure that people who are referred actually get seen quickly," she said. "But prevention is far cheaper than treatment. If we can stop even a handful of strokes, the scheme pays for itself." The pilot is due to be reviewed in the fall, and health officials in several other cities are said to be watching closely. In the meantime, organizers are encouraging anyone over forty who has not had their blood pressure checked in the last year to drop in. "It takes a quarter of an hour," said Mr. Clarke. "There's really no excuse."

en/en_us_kristin_medium/de/dee6b431ce74b.text: Imagine receiving a letter that says you have been randomly selected to help decide a difficult public question. You will spend several weekends listening to experts, discussing evidence with ninety-nine strangers and, finally, voting on recommendations that will be sent to the government. Your travel and accommodation will be paid for. You are not required to accept — but would you? This is how a citizens' assembly works, and over the past two decades, assemblies like this have been used by national governments, regions and cities around the world. The idea is surprisingly old. In ancient Athens, many public officials were chosen by lottery rather than by election, partly because lotteries were considered harder to manipulate. A modern assembly usually brings together between fifty and one hundred and fifty people. Members are not chosen completely at random. Invitations are sent to thousands of households, and from those who reply, a final group is selected so that it reflects the population in terms of age, gender, region, education and other factors. The aim is a "mini-public": a small group that looks like the country or city as a whole. Supporters argue that assemblies offer something that ordinary politics struggles to provide: time to think. Members are given balanced information, hear from people with opposing views and discuss the issues in small groups led by trained facilitators. Because they do not need to win elections or raise money, they are free to change their minds. Many participants report that the experience changed how they see people who disagree with them. "I came in sure that I was right," one member of a regional assembly on transport told researchers. "I left understanding why other people saw it differently." Critics raise several concerns. Assemblies are expensive and slow, and their recommendations are usually not binding: governments can accept them, change them or ignore them entirely. If recommendations are repeatedly ignored, it is argued, participants and the public may become more cynical, not less. Others question whether a small group of randomly selected people, however representative, should have so much influence over decisions that affect millions. The way a question is framed, and which experts are invited, can also shape the outcome. Most researchers see assemblies not as a replacement for elected parliaments, but as a complement to them — a tool that is particularly useful for long-term or complex issues on which politicians find it hard to agree. Their success seems to depend heavily on design: a clear question, enough time, independent organization and a firm commitment from the government to respond publicly to every recommendation. So, would you accept the invitation? Many people say they would. In practice, however, only a small fraction of those invited reply to the letter. Perhaps that is the real test of the idea: not whether ordinary people can make good decisions, but whether enough of them are willing to give up their weekends to try.

en/en_us_kristin_medium/e8/e8b9539d0a588.text: Ten years ago, Marta Lindqvist would not have been seen dead in secondhand clothes. "I associated them with not having enough money," the twenty-nine-year-old accountant admits. Today, almost everything she wears was owned by someone else first, and she sells the clothes she no longer wants through an app on her phone. "If I hadn't started buying secondhand, I'd have a wardrobe full of things I never wear — and a lot less money in the bank." Marta is part of a quiet revolution. The resale market — clothes, furniture, electronics and even toys sold from one consumer to another — has grown rapidly in recent years, and some analysts predict that secondhand clothing could one day rival fast fashion in size. Online platforms have made it easy to buy and sell in minutes, and the stigma that once surrounded used goods has largely disappeared, especially among younger shoppers. The reasons are partly financial. With rents and food prices rising in many countries, buying a nearly new coat for a third of the original price is an obvious choice. But for many buyers, the motivation is environmental. The fashion industry is responsible for a significant share of global carbon emissions and water pollution, and extending the life of a garment by even a few months can reduce its environmental impact considerably. Not everyone is convinced that the boom is entirely positive, however. Some critics point out that easy resale can encourage people to buy even more, simply because they know they can sell things again. "If you buy ten dresses because you can resell nine of them, you haven't really changed your habits," says Dr. Anil Rao, who researches consumer behavior. "You've just found a new way to shop." Others worry that professional resellers buy up the cheapest items in charity shops, leaving less for people who genuinely depend on them. Alongside the resale market, another trend is growing: repair. In cities across Europe and North America, volunteer-run "repair cafés" invite people to bring broken toasters, lamps and bicycles and fix them with the help of experts. In some places, governments have introduced "right to repair" rules, which require manufacturers to make spare parts available for longer. For economists, these trends raise an interesting question. Economies have traditionally measured success by how much is produced and sold. If people buy fewer new things and keep them longer, sales of new goods may fall — even if people's quality of life improves. Some businesses are already adapting by offering repairs, rentals or buy-back schemes alongside their new products. Marta, for her part, has no plans to go back. "I still love clothes," she says. "I just love them for longer now."

es/dialogue/03/03376352373a7965.mp3.text:
f:Mis amigos de Milán creen que en España todo el mundo duerme la siesta.
f:¡Ojalá! Si durmiera la siesta todos los días, llegaría tarde al trabajo.
m:En Mánchester me preguntan si aquí la gente cena a medianoche.
f:Bueno, eso tiene algo de verdad. Si cenas a las diez, aquí eres normal.
f:Y hablan de los españoles como si todos bailarais flamenco todos los días.
f:Pues yo soy de Granada y no sé bailar flamenco. ¡Ni sevillanas!
m:A mí me pasa algo parecido. Todos piensan que en Mánchester solo hablamos de fútbol.
f:¿Y los italianos? Si fuéramos como en las películas, gritaríamos todo el día.
f:¡Ja, ja! Bueno, todos los tópicos tienen algo de verdad, ¿no?
m:Sí, pero si conoces a la gente, ves que cada persona es distinta.
f:Exacto. Si todo el mundo viajara más, habría muchos menos prejuicios.
f:Pues brindemos por eso. ¡Y si queréis, el domingo os llevo a ver flamenco auténtico!

es/dialogue/05/0534755a9868d4f1.mp3.text:
f:Bueno, ¿qué te pareció la chica que vino ayer a ver la habitación?
m:¿Noelia? Me cayó muy bien. Es abierta y parece muy de fiar.
f:A mí también. Además, fue la única que preguntó por las tareas de casa.
m:Sí, eso me gustó. El chico con el que hablamos el lunes no preguntó nada.
f:Es que ese chico era un poco egoísta, ¿no? Solo hablaba de sí mismo.
m:Hombre, a lo mejor era tímido. Hay gente que habla mucho cuando está nerviosa.
f:Puede ser. Por cierto, Noelia es enfermera en el hospital donde trabaja mi hermana.
m:¡Qué casualidad! ¿Y qué dice tu hermana de ella?
f:Que es muy sensata, muy generosa y que siempre está de buen humor.
m:Pues no hay más que hablar. ¿La llamas tú o la llamo yo?
f:La llamo yo ahora mismo. ¡Por fin tenemos compañera de piso!

es/dialogue/06/069bf3bf961f3861.mp3.qaTranscript: Hola, buenas tardes. puedo ayudarle. Sí, quería ver los zapatos marrones del escaparate. ¿Qué número usa? El 42. Un momento aquí tiene, ¿qué tal? Me quedan un poco pequeños. Tiene el 43. En marrón no, lo siento, pero tengo el 43 en negro. ¿Puedo probarme los nérolos? Claro, ¿qué tal le quedan? Muy bien. ¿Cuánto cuesta? 80 y 9 euros, pero hoy hay un descuento del 20%. Entonces cuesta en 71 .20. Exacto, para contar jetón efectivo. Contajeta, me lo ciego.
es/dialogue/06/069bf3bf961f3861.mp3.text:
f:Hola, buenas tardes. ¿Puedo ayudarle?
m:Sí, quería ver los zapatos marrones del escaparate.
f:¿Qué número usa?
m:El cuarenta y dos.
f:Un momento… Aquí tiene. ¿Qué tal?
m:Me quedan un poco pequeños. ¿Tiene el cuarenta y tres?
f:En marrón, no. Lo siento. Pero tengo el cuarenta y tres en negro.
m:¿Puedo probarme los negros?
f:Claro. ¿Qué tal le quedan?
m:Muy bien. ¿Cuánto cuestan?
f:Ochenta y nueve euros, pero hoy hay un descuento del veinte por ciento.
m:Entonces, ¿cuestan setenta y uno con veinte?
f:Exacto. ¿Paga con tarjeta o en efectivo?
m:Con tarjeta. Me los llevo.

es/dialogue/07/07bea8d32105d0b9.mp3.text:
m:Aquí dice que tenemos que escribir cómo creemos que será el mundo cuando abran la cápsula, dentro de veinticinco años.
f:Uf, qué difícil. Yo pondría que para entonces habremos dejado de usar el coche privado en las ciudades.
m:¿Tú crees? Yo soy más pesimista. Como mucho, habremos cambiado los coches de gasolina por eléctricos.
f:Bueno, pon las dos cosas. ¿Y qué más? ¿El trabajo?
m:Apuesto a que la semana de cuatro días se habrá generalizado. Y las máquinas habrán transformado muchísimos trabajos.
f:Eso seguro. Por cierto, ¿has visto a Raúl? Dijo que vendría a las seis y ya son casi las siete.
m:Se habrá perdido, como siempre. O se habrá quedado charlando con alguien en la puerta.
f:O no se habrá acordado. Ya sabes cómo es… Bueno, sigamos. ¿Y nosotros? ¿Dónde estaremos?
m:Yo, con un poco de suerte, ya me habré jubilado y estaré viviendo en un pueblo de la sierra.
f:Pues yo espero haber cumplido mi sueño de toda la vida: abrir mi propia librería.
m:Me encanta. Lo apunto: "Ainhoa habrá abierto la librería más bonita de La Rioja".
f:¡Mira, por ahí viene Raúl! A ver qué excusa se habrá inventado esta vez.

es/dialogue/0f/0f61ec9706786a07.mp3.text:
f:Buenos días, Malik. Siéntese, por favor. ¿Ha encontrado bien el restaurante?
m:Sí, sin problema. Muchas gracias por llamarme.
f:He leído su currículum. ¿Dónde trabaja ahora?
m:Trabajo en una pizzería los fines de semana desde hace un año.
f:¿Y antes? ¿Tiene experiencia en cocina?
m:Sí, trabajé dos veranos en un hotel de Salou.
f:¿Y qué hacía allí exactamente?
m:Preparaba los desayunos y me encargaba de las ensaladas.
f:¿Y cómo era el ambiente de trabajo?
m:Muy bueno. Éramos un equipo joven y trabajábamos muy bien juntos.
f:El puesto incluye noches. ¿Está dispuesto a trabajar por la noche?
m:Sí, claro. Para mí no es ningún problema.

es/dialogue/12/12e11f0879c9f8c3.mp3.text:
f:Abuelo, ¿me ayudas con un trabajo para el cole?
m:Claro, cariño. ¿De qué es el trabajo?
f:Es sobre la infancia de los abuelos. ¿Empezamos?
m:¡Uf, hace muchos años de eso! Venga, pregunta.
f:¿Cuándo aprendiste a montar en bici?
m:A los nueve años. Me enseñó mi hermano mayor, en la plaza.
f:¿Y te caíste alguna vez?
m:¡Muchas! Un día choqué con la fuente y me caí al agua.
f:¿Al agua? ¿Y qué pasó después?
m:Mi madre oyó los gritos y llegó corriendo.
f:¿Se enfadó contigo?
m:Un poco. Pero al final me secó y me preparó un chocolate.

es/dialogue/13/136397a98a43bfad.mp3.text:
f:Bueno, ¿cómo vamos a Santiago: en tren, en autobús o en avión?
m:El autobús es la opción más barata: treinta y cinco euros.
f:Sí, pero tarda ocho horas. ¡Es el más lento de todos!
m:¿Y el avión? Es el más rápido.
f:Rápido, sí, pero los billetes están carísimos esta semana.
m:Entonces el tren. Tarda unas tres horas y media.
f:Y es el más cómodo. Puedo leer y trabajar un poco.
m:¿Cuánto cuesta?
f:Sesenta euros, pero hay una oferta si compramos hoy.
m:¿Y alquilamos un coche allí? Así podremos ver la costa.
f:Buena idea. Para mí, el tren y un coche allí es la mejor opción.
m:Vale, me has convencido. ¡Compramos los billetes ahora mismo!

es/dialogue/14/146493c827450a61.mp3.text:
m:Bienvenida, Mariana. ¿Qué tal tu primer día?
f:Bien, aunque un poco nerviosa. ¿Cuánto tiempo hace que trabajas aquí?
m:Trabajo aquí desde hace ocho años. Empecé de botones.
f:¿De botones? ¿Y desde cuándo eres recepcionista?
m:Desde 2020. Ahora también me encargo de las reservas de grupos.
f:¿Y cuándo hay más trabajo en la recepción?
m:Entre las once y las dos, con las salidas y las llegadas.
f:¿Y los turnos? ¿Cambian cada semana?
m:Sí, una semana de mañana y otra de tarde.
f:¿También hay turno de noche?
m:Sí, pero es de Raimundo. Hace diez años que trabaja de noche.
f:¡Diez años de noche! ¡Qué valiente!

es/dialogue/16/16c42fe0bcebae04.mp3.text:
f:¿Hamid Ziani? Hola, soy Lourdes, del campamento Los Pinos.
m:Sí, soy yo. ¡Buenos días!
f:Buenos días. Le llamo por su solicitud para monitor de verano. ¿Tiene unos minutos?
m:Sí, claro. Dígame.
f:En su currículum pone que estudia Magisterio. ¿En qué curso está?
m:Estoy en tercero. Quiero ser maestro de primaria.
f:Muy bien. ¿Ha trabajado antes con niños?
m:Sí. El verano pasado trabajé dos meses en un campamento en Huesca. Organizaba juegos y excursiones para niños de ocho a doce años.
f:¿Y qué era lo más difícil?
m:Al principio, la hora de dormir. ¡Nunca querían acostarse!
f:Ja, ja, es normal. ¿Habla inglés? Este año vienen niños de Irlanda.
m:Sí, tengo un B2. Y también hablo árabe.
f:Perfecto. El puesto es del uno al treinta y uno de julio, y hay que dormir en el campamento.
m:No hay problema. ¿El alojamiento y la comida están incluidos?
f:Sí, y el sueldo es de novecientos euros al mes. ¿Podría venir el jueves a una entrevista con el director?
m:Sí, el jueves me viene bien. ¿A qué hora?
f:A las diez. Le mando la dirección por correo electrónico.

es/dialogue/18/184a78a98adc3f5c.mp3.qaTranscript: Hotel Marafull buenas tardes. Hola, ¿qué rías reservar una habitación doble? Para que fechas. Del viernes doce al domingo 14. Dos noches, entonces, ¿cuántas personas son? Dos, ¿cuánto cuesta la habitación? 90 ebulos por noche con desayuno. ¿A qué odia es el desayuno? De siete a diez y media. La habitación tiene aire acondicionado. Sí, y una terraza con vistas al mar. genial mi nombre es Kimle
es/dialogue/18/184a78a98adc3f5c.mp3.text:
m:Hotel Mar Azul, buenas tardes.
f:Hola. Quería reservar una habitación doble.
m:¿Para qué fechas?
f:Del viernes doce al domingo catorce.
m:Dos noches, entonces. ¿Cuántas personas son?
f:Dos. ¿Cuánto cuesta la habitación?
m:Noventa euros por noche, con desayuno.
f:¿A qué hora es el desayuno?
m:De siete a diez y media.
f:¿La habitación tiene aire acondicionado?
m:Sí, y una terraza con vistas al mar.
f:¡Genial! Mi nombre es Kim Lee.

es/dialogue/1a/1a9754e1d5e9ef28.mp3.text:
f:Buenas tardes y bienvenidos a "La tarde en casa". Hoy hablamos del tiempo que pasamos delante de las pantallas. Tenemos la primera llamada. ¿Hola?
m:Hola, Celia. Me llamo Gonzalo y llamo desde Burgos.
f:Hola, Gonzalo. Cuéntanos, ¿cuántas horas pasas tú con el móvil?
m:Pues la verdad es que muchas. El otro día miré el tiempo de pantalla y casi me caigo de la silla: seis horas al día.
f:¡Seis horas! ¿Y en qué las pasas?
m:Sobre todo en redes sociales y viendo vídeos. Pero lo que me preocupa de verdad no soy yo, sino mi hijo.
f:¿Cuántos años tiene?
m:Catorce. Antes de tener móvil, jugaba al baloncesto y quedaba con sus amigos en el parque. Ahora se pasa la tarde encerrado en su habitación.
f:¿Y habéis hablado con él?
m:Sí, muchas veces, pero dice que todos sus amigos hacen lo mismo y que nosotros también estamos todo el día con el móvil. Y en eso tiene razón.
f:Es un problema muy común. Muchas gracias, Gonzalo. Tenemos otra llamada. Hola, ¿con quién hablo?
f:Hola, soy Inma, de Huelva. Quería contar lo que hicimos en mi casa, por si a Gonzalo le sirve.
f:Adelante, Inma.
f:Hace un año pusimos una norma: durante las comidas y después de las diez de la noche, nadie usa el móvil. Ni los niños ni los adultos.
f:¿Y funcionó?
f:Al principio fue un desastre. Mi hija se enfadaba muchísimo y mi marido siempre tenía una excusa del trabajo. Pero al cabo de un mes, todos nos habíamos acostumbrado.
f:¿Y qué ha cambiado desde entonces?
f:Hablamos mucho más durante la cena y dormimos mejor. Además, los sábados por la mañana hacemos algo juntos sin pantallas: una excursión, un juego de mesa…
f:Me parece una idea estupenda. ¿Le recomiendas algo más a Gonzalo?
f:Sí, que dé ejemplo. Si los padres no dejamos el móvil, es imposible pedírselo a los hijos.
f:Muy buen consejo. Gracias, Inma. Seguimos después de la publicidad.

es/dialogue/1b/1b6d8e27680a70b6.mp3.qaTranscript: Perdone, ¿cuánto cuesta la chaqueta verde? 40 y 5 euros. 45. Es un poco cara. Para usted, 40. Y las camisetas, ¿cuánto cuesta? 12 euros cada una o 3 por 30. Qué bien, quiero 3 camisetas. ¿De qué colobes? Una blanca, una negra y una roja. Muy bien, son 70 euros en total. ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? No, lo siento, sólo en efectivo.
es/dialogue/1b/1b6d8e27680a70b6.mp3.text:
m:Perdone, ¿cuánto cuesta la chaqueta verde?
f:Cuarenta y cinco euros.
m:¿Cuarenta y cinco? Es un poco cara.
f:Para usted, cuarenta.
m:¿Y las camisetas? ¿Cuánto cuestan?
f:Doce euros cada una, o tres por treinta.
m:¡Qué bien! Quiero tres camisetas.
f:¿De qué colores?
m:Una blanca, una negra y una roja.
f:Muy bien. Son setenta euros en total.
m:¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?
f:No, lo siento, solo en efectivo.

es/dialogue/1d/1d16323539d53628.mp3.text:
f:Pase, pase. Siéntese. Dígame, ¿qué le pasa?
m:Me duele mucho la garganta y anoche tuve fiebre.
f:A ver, abra la boca, por favor… Sí, tiene una infección.
m:¿Es grave, doctora?
f:Tranquilo, no es grave. ¿Es usted alérgico a algún medicamento?
m:Sí, soy alérgico a la penicilina.
f:Muy bien. Le receto otro antibiótico y un jarabe para la tos.
m:¿Y cuántas veces al día?
f:Una pastilla cada ocho horas, y el jarabe después de comer.
m:¿Puedo ir a trabajar mañana?
f:Mejor no. Descanse dos días y beba mucha agua.
m:De acuerdo. Muchas gracias, doctora.

es/dialogue/1d/1d16fa15ac25c171.mp3.text:
m:Nuria, necesito a alguien que me explique un chiste. Mi compañero de piso lo contó ayer y todos se rieron menos yo.
f:A ver, cuéntamelo. Aunque te advierto que un chiste explicado pierde toda la gracia.
m:Uno pregunta: "¿Está listo tu hermano?". Y el otro contesta: "Listo es, pero vestido todavía no".
f:¡Ja! Es un juego de palabras con ser y estar. Estar listo es estar preparado, y ser listo es ser inteligente.
m:¡Ah, claro! O sea, que el hermano es muy inteligente, pero todavía no está preparado para salir. ¡Qué bueno!
f:Exacto. Con ser y estar hay un montón de chistes: no es lo mismo ser rico que estar rico, ni ser malo que estar malo.
m:Pues yo intenté hacer una broma en clase la semana pasada y no hubo nadie que se riera. Silencio total.
f:¿Por qué? ¿Qué dijiste?
m:Llegué tarde y, para disculparme, dije que estaba muy embarazado. Quería decir que me daba vergüenza.
f:¡Ay, Lukas! Embarazado significa que esperas un bebé. Ahora entiendo el silencio… y seguro que alguna risa contenida.
m:Pues la próxima vez, el que se ría de mí invita a las cañas.
f:Trato hecho. Pero quien ríe el último ríe mejor, y tú ya tienes una anécdota buenísima para contar.

es/dialogue/20/20a32c45e78c725b.mp3.qaTranscript: Buenos didas, señor Herrera. Buenos didas, Lucida. ¿Cómo está usted? Muy bien, gracias. Y usted? Bien, bien, gracias. Hola, Lucía, Quetzal. Hola, Javi, bien y tú. Regular, estoy muy cansado hoy. Vaya ánimo. Hasta mañana, Lucía. Hasta mañana, señor Herrera. Hasta luego, Lucía.
es/dialogue/20/20a32c45e78c725b.mp3.text:
f:Buenos días, señor Herrera.
m:Buenos días, Lucía. ¿Cómo está usted?
f:Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y usted?
m:Bien, bien, gracias.
m:¡Hola, Lucía! ¿Qué tal?
f:¡Hola, Javi! Bien, ¿y tú?
m:Regular… Estoy muy cansado hoy.
f:¡Vaya! ¡Ánimo!
m:Hasta mañana, Lucía.
f:Hasta mañana, señor Herrera.
m:¡Hasta luego, Lucía!

es/dialogue/22/22535cec21a8ae03.mp3.text:
f:Papá, ¿tú qué habrías estudiado si hubieras podido elegir libremente?
m:Música, sin duda. Si mis padres no hubieran insistido tanto, habría ido al conservatorio de Madrid.
f:¿Y por qué les hiciste caso? Ya eras mayor de edad.
m:Porque en aquella época no me atreví a llevarles la contraria. Ojalá hubiera tenido tu valentía.
f:¿Te arrepientes de haber estudiado Derecho?
m:A veces sí, no te voy a engañar. Pero, si no hubiera estudiado Derecho, no habría conocido a tu madre en la facultad.
f:Y yo no estaría aquí, claro. Visto así, menos mal que les hiciste caso.
m:¡Exacto! Además, si hubiera sido músico, quizás ahora estaría harto de la música. Nunca se sabe.
f:Pues yo tengo miedo de equivocarme. ¿Y si elijo Bellas Artes y dentro de diez años me arrepiento?
m:Mira, si algo me ha enseñado la vida es que casi todo tiene arreglo. Yo empecé a tocar en un grupo a los cincuenta.
f:Es verdad, y os va genial. De haberlo sabido, ¿habrías empezado mucho antes?
m:Sin duda. Esa es mi lección: no esperes treinta años para hacer lo que te gusta. Elige lo que te ilusione.

es/dialogue/22/226ee46ff9ded4dd.mp3.text:
f:Abuela, este arroz al horno está buenísimo. ¿Me pasas el pan, por favor?
f:Toma, aquí te lo dejo. Kenji, ¿te pongo un poco más?
m:Sí, por favor, un poquito más. Es la primera vez que lo pruebo.
f:Pues es una receta de mi madre. Me la enseñó cuando yo tenía doce años.
m:¿Me la escribes? Me encantaría hacérselo a mis padres en Japón.
f:Claro que sí, hijo. Te la escribo después del café.
f:Abuela, ¡a mí nunca me la has querido dar! ¡Qué injusticia!
f:Porque tú nunca me la has pedido, guapa.
f:Bueno, pues ahora te la pido. Kenji, ¿me pasas el vino?
m:Toma. ¿Y el postre? ¿Quién lo ha traído?
f:Lo he comprado yo en la pastelería de abajo. ¿Os lo sirvo ya?
f:Sí, sírvelo ya, que luego viene lo mejor: la sobremesa.

es/dialogue/26/26b2b23f69b36492.mp3.text:
m:Chloé, ¿al final vas a venir a las Fallas?
f:¡Sí! Llegaré a Valencia el dieciocho por la mañana.
m:¡Genial! Ese día habrá mucha gente en el centro.
f:¿Y qué veremos? No sé mucho de las Fallas.
m:A las dos iremos a la mascletà, en la plaza del Ayuntamiento.
f:¿La mascletà? ¿Qué es eso?
m:Son petardos: mucho ruido durante unos minutos. ¡Te encantará!
f:¿Y las fallas? ¿Son esas figuras gigantes?
m:Sí. Las quemarán la noche del diecinueve.
f:¿Las queman todas? ¡Qué pena!
m:Es la tradición. Después cenaremos buñuelos con chocolate.
f:Vale, pero llevaré tapones para los oídos.

es/dialogue/28/284413d15ad8b919.mp3.text:
f:Hugo, ¿ya has mirado sitios para el puente de mayo?
m:Sí, tengo tres opciones: Cabo de Gata, los Pirineos o Lisboa.
f:¿Cuál es la más barata?
m:Cabo de Gata. Hay un apartamento por sesenta euros la noche, y podemos ir en coche.
f:¿Y los Pirineos?
m:Una casa rural preciosa, pero es la opción más cara: ciento veinte euros la noche.
f:¡Carísima! ¿Y Lisboa?
m:El hotel es barato, pero los vuelos están carísimos en mayo.
f:Entonces, Cabo de Gata. Tiene las playas más bonitas de Almería.
m:Sí, pero ¿y si hace mal tiempo?
f:En mayo, en Almería, casi nunca llueve.
m:Bueno. Si hace frío para bañarnos, haremos senderismo por el parque natural.
f:Perfecto. ¿Reservas tú el apartamento?
m:Vale. Si lo reservo hoy, nos hacen un descuento del diez por ciento.
f:¡Pues resérvalo ya! Yo miraré restaurantes.
m:¡Hecho! Va a ser el mejor puente del año.

es/dialogue/2e/2e6f47f423dc4ecb.mp3.text:
f:Bueno, ¿qué os ha parecido "El verano de los relojes"? Guillermo, empieza tú.
m:A mí me ha encantado. Lo mejor son los personajes, sobre todo la abuela.
f:Pues a mí me ha costado mucho terminarlo. Lo malo es que tiene demasiadas descripciones.
f:Es verdad que el principio es lento. Pero ¿qué os pareció el final?
m:Lo más sorprendente es que el narrador era el reloj de la abuela. ¡No me lo esperaba!
f:Eso sí me gustó. Lo que no entendí es por qué la autora cambia tanto de época.
f:Yo creo que lo importante en la novela es la memoria. Por eso salta de una época a otra.
m:Además, mientras lo leía, escuchaba los boleros que salen en el libro. ¡Qué maravilla!
f:¿Boleros? Yo soy más de pop, la verdad. Pero me apunto la idea de leer con música.
f:Pues para la próxima reunión propongo un libro de cuentos, que es más corto.
f:¡Me parece genial! Lo peor de este mes ha sido no tener tiempo para leer.
m:Venga, pues cuentos. Y yo me encargo de traer la música.

es/dialogue/2f/2f7cfd8c43f44157.mp3.text:
f:¡Hola, Mauro! ¿Qué tal? Oye, ¿qué haces en Nochevieja?
m:Pues todavía no lo sé. ¿Por qué?
f:Haremos una cena en mi casa con unos amigos. ¿Te gustaría venir?
m:¡Me encantaría! ¿Cuántos seremos?
f:Ocho, más o menos. Cenaremos a las nueve y media y después veremos las campanadas en la tele.
m:¿Y tomaremos las uvas?
f:¡Claro! Yo compraré las uvas. ¿Podrías traer el cava?
m:Sin problema. ¿Llevo también algo de postre?
f:No, mi madre nos hará turrón casero. ¡Está buenísimo!
m:¡Qué bien! ¿Y después de cenar?
f:A la una saldremos a una fiesta en el centro. Habrá música hasta las seis.
m:Uf, ¿hasta las seis? El día uno tengo una comida familiar a las dos…
f:Bueno, si estás cansado, puedes volver a casa antes.
m:Vale. Entonces nos vemos el treinta y uno a las nueve.
f:¡Perfecto! Y ponte algo rojo: dicen que da buena suerte.

es/dialogue/2f/2fce59d150d0c028.mp3.text:
f:¡Hola, Darío! ¡Qué moreno estás! ¿Qué tal las vacaciones?
m:¡Genial! Fuimos a Galicia, a las Rías Baixas.
f:¡Qué bien! ¿Y dónde estuvisteis?
m:En una casa rural cerca de Pontevedra. Estuvimos diez días.
f:¿Y qué tal el tiempo? Allí llueve mucho, ¿no?
m:Tuvimos suerte: solo llovió un día.
f:¿Y qué hicisteis?
m:Hicimos una excursión en barco a las islas Cíes. ¡Qué pasada!
f:Dicen que las playas son preciosas.
m:Sí, pero el agua, fría, fría. Mi marido no quiso bañarse.
f:¿Y la comida? ¿Probasteis el pulpo?
m:Sí, y Martín pidió marisco todos los días.

es/dialogue/33/33e1ae180f61e735.mp3.text:
f:Unai, son las siete y media. ¡Arriba!
m:Mamá, no puedo ir al instituto. Estoy fatal.
f:¿Qué te pasa, cariño?
m:Me duele mucho la cabeza y también la garganta.
f:A ver… No tienes fiebre. ¿Te duele algo más?
m:Sí, me duele el estómago. Y estoy un poco mareado.
f:¡Vaya! ¿Ayer cenaste mucho?
m:No, casi nada. Y anoche dormí muy mal.
f:Qué raro… Oye, ¿hoy no tienes el examen de mates?
m:Eh… sí. ¿Por qué?
f:Porque a tu hermana le duele la cabeza antes de cada examen.
m:Vale, vale… Ya me levanto.

es/dialogue/35/35df2afce9490a4c.mp3.text:
f:No te lo vas a creer: me ha llegado una carta del juzgado. Me ha tocado ser candidata a jurado.
m:¿En serio? Me sorprende que te hayan elegido a ti, con lo poco que te gustan las series de juicios.
f:Muy gracioso. Se elige por sorteo entre todas las personas inscritas en el censo electoral.
m:Ya. ¿Y no puedes librarte? Con el trabajo que tenemos este trimestre…
f:Solo por motivos muy concretos, y el trabajo no es uno de ellos. Además, es un deber como ciudadana.
m:Hombre, visto así… Me parece bien que te lo hayas tomado con tanta responsabilidad.
f:Lo que me preocupa es no estar a la altura. No creo que me hayan elegido por mis conocimientos de derecho.
m:Precisamente se trata de eso: de que decidan personas normales, no expertos. La parte técnica es cosa de los jueces.
f:Es verdad. Y me alegra que mi madre me haya contado su experiencia: fue jurado hace años y dice que aprendió muchísimo.
m:¿Y la empresa? Espero que en Recursos Humanos te hayan contestado ya.
f:Sí, esta mañana. Me han dicho que es un derecho del trabajador y que me pagarán esos días con normalidad.
m:Pues entonces, enhorabuena. Cuando termine el juicio, quiero que me lo cuentes todo… bueno, lo que puedas.

es/dialogue/38/384a381c2d1dbccc.mp3.qaTranscript: Pau, ¿qué hora es? Son las ocho menos cuarto. Vuf, mi clase es a las ocho y media. Tranquila, el ámptobus pasa a las ocho. ¿A qué hora termina soy? Termino a las tres de la tarde. ¿Y tú? Yo a la una y media. Comemos juntos a las tres y cuarto. Vale, en el bar de la esquina. Madina, son las ocho menos cinco. Adiós, adiós, hasta luego.
es/dialogue/38/384a381c2d1dbccc.mp3.text:
f:Pau, ¿qué hora es?
m:Son las ocho menos cuarto.
f:¡Uf! Mi clase es a las ocho y media.
m:Tranquila, el autobús pasa a las ocho.
f:¿A qué hora terminas hoy?
m:Termino a las tres de la tarde. ¿Y tú?
f:Yo, a la una y media.
m:¿Comemos juntos a las tres y cuarto?
f:¡Vale! En el bar de la esquina.
m:¡Marina, son las ocho menos cinco!
f:¡Adiós, adiós! ¡Hasta luego!

es/dialogue/3b/3b4c21126aaba4cd.mp3.text:
f:¡Por fin hemos terminado la carrera! ¿Qué vas a hacer ahora, Teo?
m:En septiembre voy a empezar un máster en Barcelona.
f:¡Qué bien! ¿Y después? ¿Volverás a Almería?
m:No lo sé. A lo mejor me quedo en Barcelona. ¿Y tú?
f:Yo voy a trabajar un año para ahorrar dinero.
m:¿Para qué? ¿Tienes algún plan?
f:Sí. Mi sueño es viajar por Sudamérica: Perú, Bolivia, Chile…
m:¡Qué envidia! ¿Y dónde te ves dentro de diez años?
f:Seguro que viviré cerca del mar. Probablemente aquí, en Almería.
m:Yo creo que tendré un perro y una casa en el campo.
f:¿Tú, en el campo? ¡Pero si odias los bichos!
m:Bueno, a lo mejor me compro solo el perro.

es/dialogue/3d/3dbc33de984b449b.mp3.text:
m:Nuria, mañana empiezo la carrera y estoy hecho un flan.
f:Es normal, Adrián. ¡Pero no te preocupes tanto! Te va a encantar Santiago.
m:¿Qué me recomiendas para los primeros días? No conozco a nadie.
f:Te recomiendo que vayas a todas las actividades de bienvenida de la facultad.
m:¿Y si no hablo con nadie? Ya sabes que soy bastante tímido.
f:Por eso es importante que des tú el primer paso con los compañeros.
m:Vale. ¿Y con el dinero? Mamá dice que soy un desastre.
f:Te aconsejo que hagas un presupuesto cada mes. Y no comas fuera todos los días.
m:¿Y para estudiar? En el instituto siempre lo dejaba todo para el final.
f:Pues no dejes nada para el último momento. Es mejor que estudies un poco cada día.
m:Lo intentaré. Gracias, Nuria, eres la mejor hermana del mundo.
f:De nada. Y no te olvides de llamar a mamá de vez en cuando, ¿eh?

es/dialogue/40/409f5119c09990af.mp3.text:
f:Ernesto, este verano hemos tenido tres olas de calor. ¿Es casualidad o va a seguir pasando?
m:No es casualidad. Las olas de calor son más frecuentes debido al aumento de la temperatura media del planeta.
f:Pero mucha gente dice que en Sevilla siempre ha hecho calor en verano.
m:Y es verdad. Pero ya que el punto de partida es más alto, cada ola de calor es ahora más intensa y dura más.
f:¿Y por qué se insiste tanto en reducir emisiones si el problema es global?
